briefs.competency: predict the position and shape of the Philippine Archipelago in 50 million years, based on the current velocity of the Philippine Plate
existing_facts_en: At divergent ridges, new seafloor spreads outward at a slow but steady rate of about 2 to 20 centimeters per year.
The Philippine archipelago may change its position and appearance after 50 million years because the tectonic plates beneath it keep moving.

How fast do the plates at the Philippine Trench move?

Very slowly! Only a few centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. But over millions of years, this shapes the sea!

briefs.competency: describe the similarities and differences between electric motors and electric generators
existing_facts_en:
What is the exact opposite of an electric motor?

A generator! It makes electricity from motion, doing the exact opposite of what a motor does.
A motor and a generator are almost the same machine, but they work in reverse! One makes motion from electricity, and the other makes electricity from motion.

How do electric cars save energy when braking?

In electric cars, the motor can act as a generator when braking, so some energy is returned to the battery!

briefs.competency: explain that the ecosystem's population growth slows down as it gets closer to the carrying capacity
existing_facts_en: When a population gets crowded, density-dependent limiting factors like disease and competition for food become stronger and slow its growth.

What happens as a population grows?

A population grows fast until it hits the limit its environment can support — then growth slows down and levels off.

What happens if animal numbers stay at carrying capacity?

If the number of animals stays at the carrying capacity, the place has enough time to keep replacing its food.

briefs.competency: participate in guided activities to discover and predict how rigid and soft objects can be moved and/or changed in shape
existing_facts_en: When you squeeze clay with your hands, the force changes its shape, making it flat or forming a new figure.

Can a force change the shape of something?

Yes! A force can change an object's shape, like when you squish and squash modeling clay with your hands.
A coil spring works in tension when stretched apart, or in compression when squeezed together. It's flexible both ways!

briefs.competency: draw a simple food chain using living things from the Philippines and label them as herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores
existing_facts_en: A food chain from the Philippines could be: rice plant eaten by a rat, which is then eaten by a Philippine cobra.
People are part of food chains too — as omnivores we eat plants like rice and vegetables and animals like fish and chicken, connecting us to the Sun through our food.

What is an apex predator?

An apex predator is a carnivore at the very top of the food chain — an animal that almost nothing else hunts, like a lion or a shark.

briefs.competency: plan and carry out a scientific investigation to determine the effect of different surfaces on the size of frictional forces
existing_facts_en: In a ramp experiment, a toy car travels farthest on smooth plastic because that surface creates the least friction.
A child slips on a shiny tiled floor because the smooth surface produces very little friction between the floor and the child's shoes.

Does the size of the surface area touching affect friction?

Yes! The wider the surface area of contact, the bigger the friction. More surface touching means more rubbing between the two surfaces.

briefs.competency: demonstrate using simple models how longitudinal waves and transverse waves carry energy
existing_facts_en: A longitudinal wave can be created in a slinky by pushing and pulling one end back-and-forth in a horizontal direction.
When you move a rope up and down quickly, you create transverse waves that travel along the rope while the rope itself only moves up and down.

Is a jump rope wiggle a transverse wave?

Yes! It is a transverse wave because the rope moves up and down while the wiggle travels to the other end.

briefs.competency: make a physical model or use drawings to demonstrate how the tilt of the Earth relative to its orbit around the Sun affects the intensity of sunlight absorbed by different areas of Earth over a year
existing_facts_en: As Earth orbits the Sun, its tilt keeps pointing the same direction toward the North Star. This is exactly why our seasons change throughout the year!
Earth has seasons because it tilts on its axis as it orbits the Sun!

Why does the Northern Hemisphere experience summer in June?

Earth's tilted axis causes the Northern Hemisphere to point directly toward the Sun during June, receiving more concentrated sunlight and experiencing summer!

briefs.competency: make models of fault scenarios to illustrate: a. the epicenter of an earthquake from its focus, b. the intensity of an earthquake from its magnitude, and c. how underwater earthquakes may or may not generate tsunamis
existing_facts_en:
Where is an earthquake's shaking the strongest?

The shaking is usually strongest at the epicenter, which is the spot on the ground closest to where the quake starts!

Does every earthquake cause a tsunami?

No! It must be strong and shallow, moving the seafloor up or down. If it only slides sideways, usually no tsunami forms.
An earthquake actually starts deep underground at a point called the focus, not at the surface where the epicenter is located!

briefs.competency: gather information from the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) and other reliable websites to identify how authorities support communities affected by typhoons
existing_facts_en:
Why does PAGASA issue storm surge warnings?

To alert coastal communities and keep them safe before a typhoon arrives!
The NDRRMC is the main government agency that coordinates disaster response for floods and typhoons across the Philippines.

Who do you call for help during a typhoon?

Call 911 for emergency assistance! You can also reach the Red Cross or NDRRMC hotline for rescue and relief operations.

briefs.competency: gather information from secondary sources to name and describe the upper crustal layers of the solid earth
existing_facts_en: The crust is Earth's thinnest, outermost layer of solid rock! It's the land, mountains, and ocean floor where we live.

What rock makes up most of the land beneath our feet?

Granite! It's the main rock of continental crust, made of quartz, feldspar, and mica, with large crystals and a white-to-gray speckled look.

How thick is Earth's crust?

The oceanic crust is only about 5 kilometers thick! But the continental crust can be up to 70 kilometers thick.

briefs.competency: identify how oceanic crust and continental crust is associated with the Earth's lithospheric plates
existing_facts_en:
Did you know our oceans are growing?

Mid-ocean ridges are underwater mountains where new oceanic crust forms from rising magma! The Atlantic Ocean widens as fast as your fingernails grow each year!
Ophiolite complexes in the Philippines, like those in Zambales, are slices of ancient oceanic crust! They were thrust up onto land by plate collision.
Oceanic crust is thinner but heavier, while continental crust is thicker but lighter. When they collide, the heavier oceanic crust sinks underneath!

briefs.competency: plan a scientific investigation to verify the raw materials needed for photosynthesis
existing_facts_en: If a leaf has made food through photosynthesis, it stores some as starch, and iodine solution turns blue-black when it touches this starch.
Bromothymol blue, or BTB, is a liquid that changes color from blue to yellow when carbon dioxide makes the water more acidic.
Leaves kept in darkness show less starch than leaves exposed to light, proving that light is needed for photosynthesis to make food.

briefs.competency: represent patterns of inheritance of a simple dominant/ recessive characteristic through generations of a family
existing_facts_en:
Can a trait skip a generation?

Yes! Sometimes a child has a trait neither parent shows but a grandparent has — this happens when a hidden recessive gene passes quietly through a parent.
For most traits, a child gets two alleles—one from mom and one from dad.

What is a pedigree chart?

It's a diagram that shows how a trait passes from parents to children across several generations of a family.

briefs.competency: draw diagrams of and assemble series and parallel circuits, showing switch, battery, loads/resistors, ammeter, and voltmeter
existing_facts_en: We measure current using an ammeter! It connects right into the loop's path so current passes through it, showing in amperes how much electricity is flowing.
A voltmeter connects in parallel to measure voltage, while an ammeter connects in series! Their connection methods are completely opposite.

How do we draw a battery in a circuit diagram?

A cell is drawn as a long line (positive!) and a short line (negative!). Several cells in series? That's alternating long-short-long-short lines!

briefs.competency: carry out a valid and reliable scientific investigation to show the formation of a new substance, such as formation of a carbonate (carbon dioxide in limewater), or formation of a precipitate (from silver nitrate solution)
existing_facts_en: Carbon dioxide is the fizzy gas in soft drinks and the gas we breathe out! You can test for it because it turns limewater cloudy.

Scientists use reaction signs as real tests! Drop iodine on food with starch and it turns blue-black—that color change proves starch is there. Limewater turning cloudy is used the same way to test for carbon dioxide gas.

How do we know carbon is in our breath?

Breathe into clear limewater, and it turns cloudy! This shows your breath has carbon dioxide, made from the carbon your body used.

briefs.competency: identify modern scientific processes used to detect and measure the displacement of tectonic plates
existing_facts_en: Scientists use GPS and satellites to track the plates! They measure exactly how fast and in what direction they move.
Tectonic plates move just a few centimeters per year — about as fast as your fingernail grows! Scientists measure this slow movement using GPS satellites.
We know seafloor spreading is real because of symmetrical magnetic stripes in the rocks! The sea floor is also youngest near the ridge.

How do old rocks remember Earth's magnetic past?

When lava cools and hardens, it locks in the magnetic field's direction at that time! Scientists read this in old rocks.

briefs.competency: carry out guided investigations using different objects to describe momentum-related relationships, such as the more momentum an object has, the harder for it to stop
existing_facts_en:
Why is it harder to stop heavy or fast objects?

Because they have greater momentum! This means you need a larger force or a longer time to bring them fully to a stop.
An object with large momentum is harder to stop, so a heavy or fast vehicle needs a longer distance to fully stop!
A jeepney full of passengers is heavier, giving it more momentum and making it much harder to stop than an empty one!
A heavier moving object has more momentum at the same speed, making it harder to stop! That’s why a big truck is tougher to stop than a bicycle.

briefs.competency: recognize that scientists: a. use chemical equations to describe chemical reactions, and b. write equations in word form and using formula for common chemical reactions
existing_facts_en: When an acid meets a base, two things form: a salt and water. The basic recipe is: acid + base = salt + water!
In a chemical equation, reactants are the starting substances before a reaction. Products are the new substances formed after, and they are separated by an arrow!

How do we read a chemical equation?

Reactants go on the left of the arrow, and products on the right! The arrow simply means 'yields' or 'becomes.'

What is the simple recipe for photosynthesis?

It's carbon dioxide + water + sunlight → sugar (glucose) + oxygen! The left side has the ingredients (reactants), and the right side has the products. No atoms disappear, they just rearrange.

briefs.competency: apply the principles of conservation of mass to balance chemical equations
existing_facts_en:
How do we balance a chemical equation?

We use the inspection method: count the atoms of each element on both sides, then change the big numbers in front, called coefficients, until both sides match!
We balance a chemical equation so every atom has the same count on both sides — that's how it proves conservation of mass!
A chemical equation is balanced when each type of atom has the same number on both sides, since atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction!
We balance a chemical equation by adding coefficients! This makes sure the number of each atom is exactly the same on the reactant and product sides.

briefs.competency: use a drawing or diagram to classify some Philippine animals and plants, based on their habitat: some live on land (terrestrial), live in water (aquatic) or fly in the air (aerial)
existing_facts_en: Marine habitats are salty water places, and they include oceans, coral reefs, estuaries, the open ocean, and intertidal zones.
Aerial habitats are the spaces above the ground where animals like birds, butterflies, and bats fly and find food.

What is an aerial habitat?

An aerial habitat is a home in the air or high places, like the sky, tall trees, and other spots above the ground.
Terrestrial habitats are on land, aquatic habitats are in water, and aerial habitats are in the air or high places.

briefs.competency: make a list or draw up a table with examples of animals and plants in a particular habitat, such as a garden, rice field, seashore, and mangrove swamp
existing_facts_en: A garden is a terrestrial habitat, or land environment, where flowers like roses and tulips grow beside fruit trees like mango and papaya.
Frogs are common in Philippine rice fields, ponds, and streams, and children often see them during the rainy season.
Mangroves and coral reefs work as a team — fish grow up in the mangroves first, then move to the reef when they're bigger, so fewer mangroves mean fewer fish on the reef.
Mangroves are home to many different animals, such as fish, crabs, birds, and even monkeys and snakes.

briefs.competency: use flow charts to compare the different stages in the life cycle of animals, such as a butterfly, frog, chicken, and human
existing_facts_en: The human life cycle has five major stages: birth, infancy, childhood, adolescence, and adulthood.
A butterfly begins its life as a tiny egg, usually laid by the female butterfly on a leaf.
Humans, animals, and plants all have life cycles, but humans grow gradually without metamorphosis, while many insects and frogs change body forms completely.
A grasshopper's life cycle has three stages: it starts as an egg, hatches into a nymph that looks like a small adult without wings, and then grows into an adult with wings.

briefs.competency: plan simple scientific investigations in answering questions, such as 'Do gases (like air) or liquids (like water) have mass?', using appropriate simple science equipment, such as a balance, and a thermometer, with appropriate units
existing_facts_en:
How can you prove mass stays the same after a change?

Weigh everything before and after inside a sealed container — the weight stays exactly the same!

How do we find out an object's mass?

We use a balance to measure mass by comparing the object against known masses!
A triple beam balance is a school lab scale that measures mass accurately to tenths of a gram using three sliding weights on three beams!
To find an object's mass, put it on one balance scale pan and add known weights to the other until it balances. The total known weights equal its mass!

briefs.competency: use local information or other reliable sources to identify where the nearest active and inactive volcanoes are located and assess the risk of impacts from eruptions to their local community
existing_facts_en: Taal is one of the smallest active volcanoes in the world, but it's very dangerous because it's near many towns.
Pinatubo in Zambales is an active volcano! Many thought it was asleep, but it suddenly erupted in 1991, proving volcanoes can wake up!
Kanlaon is the highest peak in the Visayas and an active volcano on Negros Island! It often has phreatic eruptions (steam explosions) and is closely monitored by PHIVOLCS to keep locals safe.

Why was the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant (BNPP) never operated?

It was built too close to Mt. Natib, a dormant volcano, and active faults! This shows why geological hazard assessment is crucial.

briefs.competency: draw on information from secondary sources to identify situations where tidal difference could be exploited to generate renewable energy
existing_facts_en: The ocean's rise and fall of tides and waves can be turned into electricity! It’s renewable because the ocean keeps moving.
The energy from the rising and falling of ocean tides, called tidal energy, can also be turned into electricity!
Narrow Philippine straits like Sibutu Passage and San Bernardino Strait have tidal energy potential — fast sea currents could drive underwater turbines.
A tidal barrage is a huge wall built across a bay or estuary. As the tide rises and falls, the height difference drives turbines and generators to make predictable electricity!

briefs.competency: use a map and a record of tracking data to trace the path of typhoons that enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR)
existing_facts_en: Typhoon tracking predicts a typhoon's path every 6 to 12 hours over a period of at least five days.
Computer forecast models help predict typhoon motion 5 to 7 days ahead.
Weather satellites watch typhoons from space, so PAGASA can warn Filipinos before a storm arrives!
The Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) is monitored by PAGASA! If a typhoon enters or forms in the PAR, PAGASA gives it a local name.

briefs.competency: using a labeled diagram, trace how food travels through the digestive tract and explain how different digestive processes work, including mechanical processing, secretion, digestion, absorption, and elimination
existing_facts_en: Ingestion is the first process of digestion, and it simply means taking in food or any substance into the body through the mouth.
Food takes a journey: from the mouth down to the stomach, then through the long intestines where nutrients are taken in by the body.
The digestive system is made up of the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine — all working together to digest food.
Food travels from the mouth through the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine before leaving the body as waste.

briefs.competency: participate in a collaborative group or class task to examine and describe the topographical and geological evidence for plate boundaries occurring in the area where the Philippines is located
existing_facts_en:
What happens to the oceanic crust at the Manila Trench?

Gravity pulls the denser oceanic crust downward into the Earth's mantle in a geological process called subduction!

Which two large plates squeeze the Philippines?

The Philippines is squeezed right between two large plates: the Philippine Sea Plate and the Eurasian Plate!
The Philippine Trench lies along the eastern side of the Philippines, hidden beneath the Pacific Ocean!
The Philippine Trench is a subduction zone! Here, the Philippine Sea Plate sinks right beneath the Philippine plate.

briefs.competency: describe using labeled diagrams the biotic and abiotic features of tropical rainforests, swamps, estuaries, mangrove forests, and coral reefs
existing_facts_en: Some organisms hide among mangrove plants to stay away from direct sunlight or from the coldness of the water.

What touches a fish's life besides other fish?

Biotic factors, which are the living things like plants and other animals, and abiotic factors, which are the non-living things like water temperature and sunlight, both affect it!
Coral reefs need clean, shallow, warm water reached by sunlight in order to grow and thrive.

Why is the forest floor so dark?

In a tropical rainforest, the thick canopy of leaves at the top blocks almost all sunlight, making the ground dark!

briefs.competency: identify the number of valence electrons of oxygen based on its position in the periodic table
existing_facts_en: For representative elements, the group number in the periodic table tells you how many valence electrons, the electrons in the outermost shell, an atom has.
An oxygen atom has six valence electrons in its outermost shell, so it needs two more to become stable.
The electron dot diagram for oxygen shows the symbol O with six dots around it, one for each valence electron.
Oxygen, with eight electrons, has the electron configuration 1s2 2s2 2p4, giving it six valence electrons in its second energy level.

briefs.competency: use models to investigate elastic or inelastic collisions and describe the forces involved and their effects
existing_facts_en: In inelastic collisions, objects may stick together or move slower after impact because some energy is absorbed.
Billiard balls colliding on a table are a real-life example of elastic collisions because they bounce apart with almost no energy lost.
A toy car hitting clay is an inelastic collision because the clay deforms and absorbs some of the car's kinetic energy.
In an elastic collision, objects bounce apart without losing motion energy, so the total kinetic energy stays exactly the same before and after!
In an inelastic collision, objects stick together or get dented, turning some motion energy into heat and sound, but total momentum is still conserved!

briefs.competency: participate in a class debate on the societal, environmental, and ethical implications of using biotechnological products and methods
existing_facts_en: Agricultural biotechnology alters living organisms or parts of organisms to improve plants and animals, including making pest-resistant and drought-resistant crops.

Can science help clean up polluted rivers and soil?

Yes! Environmental biotechnology applies biotechnology to manage natural resources and address environmental problems like waste treatment and remediation of polluted environments.
Agricultural biotechnology uses selective breeding to improve the quality of crops like corn by choosing parent plants with the best traits.
Golden Rice is a GMO rice with extra genes that let it make beta-carotene — which the body turns into vitamin A — to help children who don't get enough.

What does GMO mean?

GMO stands for genetically modified organism — a plant or animal whose genes were changed on purpose to give it a helpful trait.

briefs.competency: make drawings or a simple model to show the motion of the Earth and Moon relative to the Sun to explain the phases of the moon that people see from Earth
existing_facts_en: The Moon has no light of its own — it reflects sunlight! As it orbits Earth, the lit part facing us changes size, giving us phases like new moon, half, and full.
At new moon, we can barely see it in the sky because its sunlit side is turned completely away from us!

Does the moon really disappear during a new moon?

Nope! The moon is always circling Earth. During a new moon, it sits between Earth and the sun, so its dark side faces us and it looks gone!
You can show Moon phases with a ball and a lamp! As the ball circles you, you see different amounts of its lit half — just like the real Moon lit by the Sun.

What happens during a new moon?

It's the start of the lunar cycle! The Moon hides between Earth and the Sun, hiding its bright side.

briefs.competency: classify common rocks from provided samples using a simple rock classification system, such as a dichotomous key
existing_facts_en: Igneous rocks are usually the hardest type of rock and often contain shiny crystals that sparkle when light hits them.
Sedimentary rocks are usually the softest type, have visible layers, and may contain fossils of ancient living things.

How do scientists identify a mystery animal?

A dichotomous key is a guide of paired either-or questions that leads you step by step to figure out which plant or animal you're looking at.

What is a dichotomous key?

It's a guide that uses paired yes-or-no questions to help you identify what kind of organism you're looking at.

What are the three main kinds of rock?

Based on how they form, there are three main kinds of rock: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks!

briefs.competency: construct a model to communicate some of the key processes in the water cycle
existing_facts_en: The water cycle has four main stages: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection, each moving water in a different way.
A sealed plastic bag with water, sand, and a rock placed in the sun can show evaporation and condensation, just like the water cycle on Earth.
A water cycle model placed in sunlight shows more evaporation and condensation than one kept in the shade.
In the water cycle, evaporation turns water into vapor, condensation turns vapor into clouds, and precipitation makes raindrops!

How does a simple bag show the water cycle?

In a water-cycle-in-a-bag experiment, the Sun's heat evaporates the water, and the vapor condenses on the cool sides to trickle down like real rain!

briefs.competency: use proper techniques in observing and identifying the parts of a cell with a microscope such as the cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, and chloroplasts
existing_facts_en: Scientists use special dyes to see cell parts clearly — iodine turns starch blue, while methylene blue reveals the nucleus.
Cytoplasm is a jelly-like fluid that fills the cell, and the cell's parts float around inside it.

Where does photosynthesis happen inside a leaf?

Inside tiny parts of leaf cells called chloroplasts! That's where the chlorophyll is, and where photosynthesis takes place.
Inside leaf cells are tiny green parts called chloroplasts! This is where photosynthesis happens and oxygen is made. The chlorophyll inside them absorbs the sun's light to get started.
Specimens under a microscope are often stained with special dyes! Staining increases the contrast between different parts so they are easier to see under light.

briefs.competency: use diagrams and illustrations to describe the arrangement, spacing, and relative motion of the particles in each of the three states (phases) of matter
existing_facts_en: When a gas is put under pressure by reducing the volume of its container, the space between particles is reduced and the gas is compressed.
Tiny particles (atoms and molecules) make up all matter and never stop moving! Solids: packed tight, just vibrating. Liquids: close but sliding. Gases: far apart and zooming fast!

Why are solids so firm?

In a solid, tiny particles are packed close together and barely move, keeping it firm!
You can't just squeeze a solid smaller! Its particles are already packed tight with almost no gaps. That's why solids keep the same volume—they can't be squished down!

Why does sound travel faster in steel than in air?

Sound travels about fifteen times faster in steel! Particles in solids are packed closer together, so they pass vibrations more quickly.

briefs.competency: relate the location and distribution of active volcanoes, earthquake epicenters, and major mountain belts to the distribution of oceanic crust and continental crust
existing_facts_en:
Where is the longest mountain range on Earth?

It's under the ocean! The mid-ocean ridge stretches thousands of kilometers along the sea floor, forming where plates pull apart and lava hardens into new rock.
Most active volcanoes form where Earth's huge plates meet! In the Philippines, on the Ring of Fire, one plate sinks under another, melting rock into magma.
When denser oceanic crust meets continental crust, it sinks because it's heavier. The melting crust creates magma that rises to form volcanoes!
Most of Earth's volcanoes are actually underwater! They sit along the Mid-Ocean Ridge, a massive mountain range hidden beneath the ocean floor.
The Ibalong Festival in Legazpi celebrates Mount Mayon! It's a perfect stratovolcano formed by tectonic plate subduction in the Pacific Ring of Fire.

briefs.competency: explain that the mechanical energy of an object is the sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy available to do work
existing_facts_en: The total energy along a track includes potential energy, kinetic energy, and dissipated forms such as heat and sound that have spread away from the moving object.
Energy lost as potential energy is gained as kinetic energy, so the total mechanical energy of a system remains the same.
Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy (from motion) and potential energy (from position). Together, they tell us an object's total energy!
Mechanical energy is the total of kinetic energy plus potential energy — without friction, this total stays the same as energy shifts between the two forms!
Mechanical energy is the total sum of an object's kinetic energy and potential energy!

briefs.competency: use models, flow charts, diagrams, and simulations to explain how body systems work together, such as digestion and excretion
existing_facts_en: Your nervous, endocrine, and circulatory systems work together to regulate temperature, glucose level, and blood pressure.

What happens if one organ system in my body stops working?

Other systems can get sick too! Your organ systems work together, so if one fails, the others are affected.
The muscular and skeletal systems work together to provide support, protection, and movement, with muscles pulling on bones to make you move.
The respiratory and circulatory systems work together to maintain homeostasis, adjusting heart rate and breathing speed based on your activity.

What stops food going into your lungs?

When you swallow, a flap called the epiglottis closes over your larynx so food doesn't go down into your lungs instead of your stomach.

briefs.competency: using flow charts and labeled diagrams explain the role of plants and animals in the cycles of nature, such as the carbon, oxygen, and water cycles
existing_facts_en: Biogeochemical cycles are nature's recycling routes, where nutrients move through living things and the air, water, and soil.
The water cycle has four main stages: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection, each moving water in a different way.
In the oxygen cycle, plants release oxygen during photosynthesis, while animals and plants use it up when they breathe — so the air's oxygen keeps getting replaced.
In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis is a crucial step! Plants absorb carbon dioxide gas and water to produce glucose and oxygen.
In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis is when plants absorb gaseous carbon dioxide to build solid glucose molecules!

briefs.competency: create a scale drawing to represent relative thicknesses of the layers of Earth's interior, including the crust, lithosphere, asthenosphere, mantle, outer core, and inner core
existing_facts_en: The mantle is the thickest layer of the Earth, a semi-solid, hot layer rich in iron, magnesium, and silicon.
Earth's mechanical layers include the crust, lithosphere, asthenosphere, mantle, outer core, and inner core.

How can we draw Earth's layers when they are so deep?

We use a scale! A scale of 1 cm = 100 km lets us shrink the huge thicknesses of Earth's layers onto paper.

How many layers does the Earth have?

The Earth has four main layers: the crust, the mantle, the outer core, and the inner core — like a giant layered ball!
Planet Earth is made of 4 main layers: the crust, the mantle, the outer core, and the inner core!

briefs.competency: use information from secondary sources to explain the beneficial, harmful, and neutral effects of mutations
existing_facts_en: Not all mutations are harmful — some are neutral with no effect, some are harmful like those causing cancer, and some are beneficial and help organisms survive.
A mutation can be helpful, harmful, or have no effect at all — most changes to genes don't hurt or help, they're just neutral.

Is a mutation always bad?

No! A mutation is a change in an organism's DNA, and it can be harmless, harmful, or even helpful for survival.

What is a mutation?

A mutation is a change in DNA — it might do nothing, help, or hurt the living thing that has it!

What is a silent mutation?

Not all mutations show. In a silent mutation, a DNA letter changes but the protein stays the same — like a typo you can still read as the same word.

briefs.competency: participate in guided activities using simple equipment to compare different types of soil including sandy, clay, silt, and loam, including comparing the ability of the soils to hold water
existing_facts_en: Clay soil has very tiny particles, which is why it holds onto water for a longer time!

Why does sandy soil dry up so fast?

Because it has larger particles! This lets water drain through it very quickly.

Why do some places have more groundwater than others?

Sand and gravel have wide spaces, so water passes through and collects easily. Clay is very tight, so water can't pass through. That's why some places have lots of groundwater and others have none!
In a soil test, clay-rich soil holds lots of water while sandy soil drains fast! This shows different soils keep different amounts of water for our plants.
Sandy soil drains water super fast after rain! But clay soil holds moisture and turns into sticky mud.

Which soil has the smallest particles and holds the most water?

It's clay! Sand, silt, and clay differ in size, but clay has the tiniest particles.

briefs.competency: participate in a guided investigation to identify the effect of different types of soil on the growth of plants
existing_facts_en:
Why is loam the best soil for crops?

Loam is best for crops because it holds just the perfect amount of water, air, and nutrients for plants!
Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline dirt is! Most crops love neutral soil with a pH of 6 to 7, but if it's too acidic, farmers can just add lime.

Why is Benguet province a perfect place to grow temperate vegetables like cabbage?

It has rich volcanic soil that creates an ideal environment for them to grow!
The abaca plant thrives in the Bicol region because its soil is rich in volcanic ash from Mount Mayon!
The purple yam, or ube, needs well-drained, loamy soils to thrive, making the volcanic and alluvial dirt of the Philippines ideal for it!

Where does the native Philippine abaca plant thrive?

It thrives in the nutrient-rich volcanic soil found right near the country's active volcanic peaks!

briefs.competency: use a table to show how living things can be classified into groups based on similar characteristics (plants including flowering and non-flowering; animals including mammals, reptiles, insects, birds, fish, amphibians; microorganisms including fungi and bacteria)
existing_facts_en:
Why do baby mammals drink milk from their mothers?

Because mammals have special body parts called mammary glands that produce milk, and this milk is the first food for their young.
Amphibians like frogs have two life stages: an aquatic gill-breathing larval stage and a terrestrial lung-breathing adult stage.

Why do we group animals like mammals, reptiles, and insects?

Because grouping them by their characteristics helps us understand how they live, what they need, and how to protect them.
Insects have jointed legs that bend at the joints, which helps them walk, jump, and climb, while animals like snakes have no legs at all.

How does a fern spread without flowers?

A fern has no flowers and no seeds—instead, it spreads using tiny spores found on the underside of its leaves.
Plants come in two big groups: flowering ones like gumamela, and non-flowering ones like ferns.

briefs.competency: draw a free-body diagram to represent the relative magnitude and direction of the forces involving balanced and unbalanced forces
existing_facts_en: In a free-body diagram of a book resting on a table, an upward normal force from the table and a downward gravitational force are drawn as equal arrows.
For a fruit falling from a tree, the free-body diagram shows only one force: a downward arrow for gravity, which is unbalanced and makes the fruit speed up.

Why do scientists draw free-body diagrams instead of just looking at a picture?

Because a free-body diagram shows only the forces, making it easier to see which forces are balanced or unbalanced!
To draw a free-body diagram, treat the object as a point, place it at the origin of an xy-coordinate system, and draw all forces as arrows from that point.

How do we draw forces?

Forces are shown using arrows, where the length stands for the strength and the point shows the direction!
A free-body diagram is a drawing that shows all the forces acting on an object, using arrows that point in the direction and size of each force!

briefs.competency: use a labelled diagram to describe the connections between the levels of biological organization to one another from cells to the biosphere
existing_facts_en: Living things are organized from smallest to largest: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and organ systems form an organism.
The correct sequence from most basic to most complex is cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, and then the whole organism.
Biological organization is like a ladder of life, arranged from the smallest parts—subatomic particles—up to the largest, the biosphere, which is all of Earth where life exists.
Biomes are very large areas with similar climate and life, like deserts or rainforests, and the biosphere is the biggest level of all—every biome on Earth where life exists.
Biological organization arranges living things from the simplest parts, like tiny molecules, to the most complex, like the entire biosphere, so scientists can study life step by step.
The biosphere is the largest level of biological organization, and it is the sum of all ecosystems on Earth where life exists.

briefs.competency: follow appropriate steps of a scientific investigation which includes: a. Aim or problem, b. Materials and equipment, c. Method or procedures, d. Results including data, and e. Conclusion
existing_facts_en: Scientific investigation is a sequential process, meaning you follow its steps in order, starting with the aim and ending with the conclusion.

What is the first thing you must state in an investigation?

You state the aim or problem, which is the purpose or reason why you are doing the activity. It can be written as a question or a statement.
The method or procedure is the series of steps you perform to obtain data, such as cutting, pounding, and squeezing the leaves to get their extract.
The conclusion is the final statement summarizing the outcomes of the investigation, like saying mayana leaves extract could be a possible alternative source of ink.

What tells you the exact steps to follow in an experiment?

The method or procedure! It is a set of instructions that guides the experimenter from start to finish.
The conclusion summarizes your findings, states whether your aim was achieved, and explains any patterns or relationships you saw in the data.

briefs.competency: gather information from secondary sources to discuss the regular occurrence of meteor showers
existing_facts_en: Meteor showers happen around the same time every year! Earth passes through the same comet dust trail annually, so astronomers know when to expect the Perseids and Geminids.

Why do some meteor showers happen at the exact same time every year?

It's because Earth passes through the same comet-debris path during each orbit!

Where do meteor showers like the Perseids and Leonids come from?

Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through a comet's debris trail! The Perseids in August come from Comet Swift-Tuttle, and the Leonids in November come from Comet Tempel-Tuttle.
Look up at the sky! The Perseid meteor shower happens every August each year.
When Earth passes through comet Swift-Tuttle's dusty trail, tiny space particles burn up in our atmosphere and create the Perseid meteor shower!

Why do meteor showers happen at the same time every year?

Earth passes through a trail of dust left by a comet! As the dust particles burn up in the atmosphere each year, we see a meteor shower!

briefs.competency: explain how the geologic time scale helps to recount the history of the Earth
existing_facts_en: The geologic time scale divides Earth's 4.5 billion-year history into eons, eras, and periods! The Precambrian is 88% of it, while dinosaurs ruled the Mesozoic era!

How is Earth's long history divided?

It's divided into major eons: Precambrian (up to 541 Ma), Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic!

How is Earth's long history divided?

In the geologic time scale, it is divided into eons, eras, periods, and epochs!
The geologic time scale organizes Earth's history into chunks: eons, eras, periods, and epochs — from the longest stretches down to the shortest!

What is a mass extinction?

It's when lots of species disappear in a short time. The rock record shows this happened several times in Earth's history!
The worst mass extinction happened about 252 million years ago at the end of the Permian period. Most species in the sea and on land died out!

briefs.competency: use models and labeled diagrams to represent the double helix structure of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid)
existing_facts_en: The two sides of the DNA ladder are a sugar-phosphate backbone, made of alternating deoxyribose sugar and phosphate groups linked together.
DNA is a double-stranded molecule shaped like a twisted ladder, with a sugar called deoxyribose and the bases A, T, C, and G.

What shape is DNA?

A twisted ladder called a double helix! Two long strands are joined together by rungs, like a spiral staircase.

What shape is DNA?

DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder — scientists call it a 'double helix'!

What shape is DNA?

DNA is shaped like a double helix — imagine a ladder that's been twisted round and round!

Who discovered the shape of DNA?

James Watson and Francis Crick discovered DNA's shape, the double helix, in 1953.

briefs.competency: explain the formation of covalent bonds using a molecule of water and a molecule of carbon dioxide
existing_facts_en: A water molecule (H₂O) has two covalent bonds! This happens because the oxygen shares electrons with each of its two hydrogen atoms.

What is a covalent bond?

In a covalent bond, two atoms share their electrons to form a molecule! It's like two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen forming water.
In IONIC bonds, electrons are GIVEN away by metals to nonmetals. But in COVALENT bonds, nonmetals SHARE electrons, just like in water! They join in totally different ways.
An ionic bond forms when atoms transfer electrons, like in NaCl (table salt). A covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons, like in H2O (water)!
A single water molecule is made of exactly two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom!
In carbon dioxide (CO₂), carbon and each oxygen share two pairs of electrons, creating a double bond between them!

briefs.competency: show by using models that ionic compounds form crystalline structures whereas covalent compounds form individual molecules
existing_facts_en: In an ionic crystal like table salt, the points of the crystal lattice are occupied by ions, which are atoms that have gained or lost electrons to get an electric charge.
Ionic compounds form a crystal lattice, a repeating three-dimensional pattern of positive and negative ions held tightly in place.
Covalent compounds form individual molecules when nonmetal atoms share electrons with each other.
Ionic bonds hold ions together in an ionic crystal, while covalent bonds hold atoms within each water molecule and weak intermolecular interactions hold water molecules together.
Look at salt under a microscope — each grain is a tiny CUBE! That's because sodium and chloride ions line up in a perfect cubic pattern.

How are ions arranged in table salt?

In NaCl, sodium and chloride ions form a repeating pattern called a crystal lattice — not separate molecules!

briefs.competency: observe and record changes in the weather during a day or over some days and describe the different types and patterns of weather in the local area
existing_facts_en: In the Philippines, thunderstorms often happen on hot afternoons when warm air rises quickly!
Mist is like a thinner fog! It makes the air hazy, but you can still see fairly far through it.
When we record weather instrument readings every day, we can spot cool patterns, like exactly when the rainy or dry season arrives!

Why does sudden rain with thunder often happen on hot afternoons in the Philippines?

That's convective rain! When the ground gets hot, warm air rises fast, forming cumulonimbus clouds that bring sudden rain and thunder.
At midday, the sun is highest with direct rays. But the hottest time is mid-afternoon—the ground and air need time to warm up!
A weather chart tracks if it's sunny, rainy, or cloudy every day, helping us spot patterns in the weather!
Towering cumulonimbus clouds produce heavy afternoon rain showers and thunderstorms that we commonly see in the Philippines!

briefs.competency: classify geological faults according to the angle of the fault plane and direction of slip
existing_facts_en: In a strike-slip fault, the two blocks of rock slide horizontally past each other, with little up or down movement.
The fault plane is the flat surface along which rocks break and move, and its angle helps identify the type of fault.
The Philippine Fault is a 'strike-slip' fault! Two huge blocks of land slide sideways past each other, like rubbing hands. When they suddenly slip, an earthquake happens!
If you stand on the Philippine Fault, the other side moves toward your left! This is called a 'left-lateral' fault, and it has been sliding this way for millions of years.

How does the Philippine Fault Zone move?

This 1,200 km long strike-slip fault crosses the Philippines! It moves horizontally in a left-lateral sense: if you stand on it and look across, the far side moves left!
The Philippine Fault is a left-lateral strike-slip fault! This means its two sides slide sideways past each other.
The Marikina Valley Fault System in Luzon is a right-lateral strike-slip fault!

briefs.competency: explain, using models, how the tilt of the Earth affects the changes in the length of daytime at different times of the year
existing_facts_en: At the poles, there are six months of daylight with no night, then six months of night! This happens because of Earth's tilt as it orbits the sun.
The tilt's effect is strongest at the poles — sometimes the Sun doesn't set for many days, and other times it barely rises at all!
Because of Earth's tilt, daylight length changes all year! Far from the equator, days are long in summer and short in winter. But in the Philippines, daylight stays about the same!
The summer solstice has the most daylight hours of the year! It happens around June 21 in the north when it tilts most toward the Sun.

What is the winter solstice and when does it happen in the north?

The winter solstice has the fewest daylight hours of the year! It happens around December 21 in the north when it tilts most away from the Sun.

Are day and night always the same length?

No! Because Earth is tilted, daylight is longer in summer and shorter in winter in most places.
Earth has seasons because it tilts on its axis as it orbits the Sun!

briefs.competency: use the PHIVOLCS FaultFinder or other reliable information source to identify where the nearest fault system is located from their community and assess the risk of earthquakes to their local community
existing_facts_en: PHIVOLCS has a free tool called FaultFinder! It shows exactly how close your house or school is to an active fault.
PHIVOLCS has a free tool called FaultFinder! It shows how close your house or school is to an active fault.

What is the West Valley Fault?

The West Valley Fault (or Marikina Valley Fault) crosses Metro Manila! PHIVOLCS warns it could cause a magnitude greater than 7.2 earthquake and widespread damage when it ruptures!

Why was the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant (BNPP) never operated?

It was built too close to Mt. Natib, a dormant volcano, and active faults! This shows why geological hazard assessment is crucial.

Why do cities like Manila and Cebu need stronger buildings?

PHIVOLCS seismic zone maps show these areas face high earthquake risk from active faults! This helps us build safer buildings and plan evacuations.
The Valley Fault System, including the Marikina segment, can generate strong earthquakes in Metro Manila!

Why is Marikina City at a high risk for strong earthquakes?

The West Valley Fault runs through Marikina City, making it highly at risk during tectonic plate movements!

briefs.competency: demonstrate proper use and handling of science equipment
existing_facts_en: Scientists wear gloves during experiments to protect their hands from heat, chemicals, and germs.

Why do some indicators need to be stored in dark places?

Strong light and air can make an indicator's color fade or spoil over time. An old or spoiled indicator gives wrong answers — so always use a fresh one!

Why do we wear gloves during experiments?

To protect our hands! They act as a barrier against heat, cuts, or chemicals while we work.
Crucible tongs safely hold a hot ceramic dish over a flame during a chemical change to prevent hand burns!

What does a glass stirring rod do in the lab?

It's a lab tool that helps mix a solute and solvent together to form a solution faster!
Want an accurate reading? Make sure your thermometer is in good contact with the thing you are measuring!

Why clean a thermometer?

We must clean a thermometer before and after use so it doesn't spread germs!

briefs.competency: predict simple ratios of offspring genotypes and phenotypes in crosses involving dominant/recessive gene pairs
existing_facts_en:
What happens when two heterozygous parents have a baby?

For one gene, the genotypic ratio of their possible offspring is 1:2:1 - one chance for homozygous dominant, two chances for heterozygous, and one chance for homozygous recessive.
To predict offspring with incomplete dominance, we still use a Punnett square — but each genotype looks different: RR is red, RW is pink, and WW is white.
When a purebred dominant parent is crossed with a purebred recessive one, all of their offspring will show the dominant trait.

What is a Punnett square used for?

A simple chart scientists use to predict the possible allele combinations offspring might get from two parents!

What ratio of traits comes from Bb x Bb parents?

When two heterozygous parents (Bb x Bb) are crossed, the offspring usually show a 3-to-1 ratio — three with the dominant trait for every one with the recessive trait.
Punnett square ratios are only probabilities, not sure things — like a coin flip, a few offspring may not match the expected ratio exactly.

What is a Punnett square used for?

It is a grid scientists use to predict the possible traits of offspring, based on the alleles of the parents.

briefs.competency: explain why humans are classified under Class Mammalia and the Order Primates
existing_facts_en: Humans belong to Order Primates, a group of mammals that includes monkeys and apes, because we share grasping hands and forward-facing eyes.
Like other primates, humans have flexible fingers and toes, nails instead of claws, and eyes that work together to judge depth.
Understanding how humans are classified with other primates helps scientists trace the shared ancestors that connect us through evolution.
Mammals, including humans, are endothermic, meaning they make their own body heat, have hair or fur, and produce milk to feed their babies.
Primates have forward-facing eyes that give them binocular vision, meaning both eyes work together to see one clear image and judge depth, which helps when jumping between branches.
Compared to their body size, primates have relatively large brains, which support their problem-solving skills, memory, and complex social lives.

What class do humans belong to?

Humans belong to the class Mammalia — that makes you a mammal too, just like dogs, cats, and whales!

briefs.competency: explain that the electron structure of an atom determines its position on the periodic table
existing_facts_en: Electron configuration, the arrangement of electrons in shells around an atom, can help determine an element's properties and its location on the periodic table.

What happens to atoms as you move down the periodic table?

Each row adds a new electron shell! Because of this, the atoms get larger as you move down.
Noble gases are completely unreactive because their outer electron shell is already totally full!
An atom's electrons are arranged in shells, or energy levels, around the nucleus. The farther a shell is from the nucleus, the higher its energy level!
The number of protons in the nucleus determines how many electrons a neutral atom has and how they are arranged! This is why each element has its own properties.
Noble gases like helium, neon, and argon are in Group 18. They almost never react because their outer electron shell is already full!
An element's period number tells exactly how many electron shells, or energy levels, its atoms have!

briefs.competency: describe different types of collisions as elastic or inelastic by providing some examples
existing_facts_en: A car crashing into a wall is an inelastic collision because the car deforms and much kinetic energy becomes sound and heat.
A dart sticking into a dartboard is an inelastic collision because the dart and board stay together after impact.
Two soccer players colliding on the field is an inelastic collision because their bodies deform slightly and they may fall together.
When a rubber ball hits the floor, it squishes and stores energy. It quickly springs back to shape, giving that energy back as an upward bounce! That is why rubber bounces, but clay does not.
In an elastic collision, objects bounce apart without losing motion energy, so the total kinetic energy stays exactly the same before and after!
In an inelastic collision, objects stick together or get dented, turning some motion energy into heat and sound, but total momentum is still conserved!
In a Newton's cradle, releasing one steel ball at the end makes just one ball fly out the far end because momentum and motion energy pass through elastic collisions!

What happens when objects crash into each other?

In some crashes, objects bounce apart! In others, they stick together and move as one big lump!

briefs.competency: participate in guided activities to locate and describe different types of non-living things found in and around their school, such as rocks, soil, water, air, metals, clouds, rain, and sunlight
existing_facts_en: Clouds come in fun shapes! Cumulus look like fluffy cotton balls, stratus form flat layers, and cirrus are high and wispy.

Why do water droplets fall from the sky as rain?

When water droplets in a cloud grow too many and too heavy, they fall back down to the ground as rain!
Dark, thick clouds are full of water! They are a clear sign that rain is coming soon.
Lenticular clouds are lens-shaped clouds that form near mountains. Because of their unusual shape, they are sometimes compared to flying UFOs!

How are clouds classified by altitude?

They are grouped by height: high clouds (cirrus), middle-level (altocumulus), and low clouds (stratus). Some, like cumulonimbus, even stretch across several levels!
Soil has cool layers! The dark, nutrient-rich topsoil is on top, subsoil is below it, and solid bedrock is at the very bottom.
Soil is made of tiny broken rock bits, sand, clay, water, air, and humus! Humus comes from rotted plants and animals, giving nutrients to growing plants.

What makes up healthy soil?

It is made of broken-down rock, organic matter called humus, water, air, and living organisms like earthworms and bacteria!

briefs.competency: assemble and draw a simple circuit using batteries, wires, switch, and bulb and/or toy motor or buzzer
existing_facts_en: Wires are the paths that connect the components of a circuit, allowing electricity to travel from the source to the bulb and back.
A simple circuit has four main parts: a source for energy, wires for a path, a switch for control, and a bulb to use the electricity.
Scientists draw circuits using special symbols! A line means wire, a short-and-long line pair means battery, and a circle with a cross means bulb. That's a circuit diagram!

What makes the current flow and lights up the bulb in a circuit?

The circuit must form a complete closed loop! If there is a gap anywhere in the wire, current cannot flow and the bulb won't light.

How do we draw a battery in a circuit diagram?

A cell is drawn as a long line (positive!) and a short line (negative!). Several cells in series? That's alternating long-short-long-short lines!

How does a switch light up a bulb?

Closing the switch completes the electrical circuit! Electrons flow from the battery through the wire to light the bulb.

How do you complete a simple electrical circuit?

Use a copper wire to connect the battery's positive terminal to the bulb, then return it to the negative terminal!
Want to light a bulb? Build a complete circuit! Electricity flows in an unbroken loop—from the battery, through the wires, to the bulb, and back again.

briefs.competency: carry out fair tests to show how levers can be used to change the magnitude and direction of a force
existing_facts_en: The handles of scissors are longer than the blades! Because of this, even a small push creates a bigger force at the blades to cut.
Scissors give you a mechanical advantage when you cut near the screw! There, the force at the blades is bigger than the push on the handles.
Is there a trade-off for a stronger blade? Yes! When cutting near the screw, the handles move a bigger distance. You trade a little distance for extra force.

How does a lever multiply your strength?

A lever spreads work over a longer distance! The farther you are from the fulcrum, the less force you need to lift heavy objects.
Lifting is easier when the lever arm to your hand is longer! That's why a crowbar has a long handle to keep you far from the fulcrum.
Torque is force multiplied by the lever arm distance! A longer lever arm produces greater torque using the exact same force.
Using a long metal crowbar to lift a rock means you push over a longer distance. This decreases your input force, but the total work stays the same!
A crowbar works as a lever—push down on the long handle, and it creates a greater upward force to lift a heavy rock!

briefs.competency: refer to the local disaster readiness plans to demonstrate what to do during and after an earthquake
existing_facts_en: Local disaster readiness plans guide what to do before, during, and after an earthquake, including checking for injuries, assessing damage, and evacuating to safe assembly areas.

Why do schools in the Philippines hold earthquake drills?

Because earthquakes are common here! During drills, we practice to duck, cover, and hold on.
Philippine schools hold earthquake drills so children can practice what to do and where to go safely during a real earthquake!
After an earthquake, check for leaking gas or broken electrical wires! These can easily start a dangerous fire.

What should you do when the earthquake shaking finally stops?

Calmly go out to an open area using the evacuation route, because there might still be aftershocks!
Earthquakes happen when tectonic plates suddenly slip, so the "drop, cover, and hold" drill is essential to protect you from falling debris!
If an earthquake strikes while you're indoors, drop to the floor, take cover under a sturdy desk, and hold on tight!
The National Earthquake Drill teaches Filipinos to drop, cover, and hold to stay safe when the West Valley Fault shakes the ground!

briefs.competency: describe procedures that the authorities have in place to alert communities of pending tsunamis and what procedures can be implemented should a tsunami impact a community
existing_facts_en: In the Philippines, PHIVOLCS watches for earthquakes. They issue a warning when a tsunami may threaten our shores!
In the Philippines, PHIVOLCS monitors earthquakes and issues warnings to keep everyone safe when there is a tsunami danger!

How do we know a tsunami is coming before it hits?

Machines and sensors in the ocean detect quakes or water changes, sending warnings so people can leave early!

How do sensors give us time to warn people about a tsunami?

Because a tsunami is low and fast in deep water, sensors can detect it while it is still far away, giving us time to warn everyone!
During a tsunami warning, boats in deep ocean water are actually safer! The wave stays small out there—it only grows tall when reaching shallow coasts.

How do seismographs help keep coastal people safe?

They give early tsunami warnings! When they detect a strong underwater earthquake, people on the coast are told to move to higher ground.
Look out for blue arrow signs in Philippine coastal areas! Installed by PHIVOLCS and local governments, these signs show exactly which way to run to safety during a tsunami.

How do we get warned about giant tsunami waves?

A deep-ocean tsunami buoy detects subtle changes in water pressure! It warns coastal areas when giant waves are approaching the shore.

briefs.competency: describe the importance of the six-kingdom system and the three-domain system of classification of living things
existing_facts_en: The three-domain system groups all life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya, based on differences in their cell structures and habitats.
Domain is the highest taxonomic rank, and kingdom is just below domain, grouping life by fundamental differences in cells and genes.
Carl Woese proposed the six-kingdom and three-domain systems by studying ribosomal RNA sequences, revealing hidden genetic differences among microbes.
The three-domain system classifies all life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya based on molecular data, especially ribosomal RNA sequences.
Scientists divide all life into three domains: Archaea and Bacteria for tiny cells without a nucleus, and Eukarya for organisms with a true nucleus.
All living things are sorted into three huge groups called domains: Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya, which includes every plant, animal, and fungus.

Is Archaea just bacteria?

No! Archaea are their own separate group of life. Like bacteria they lack a nucleus, but scientist Carl Woese used DNA to show their cell chemistry is different.
The five-kingdom system isn't frozen forever — some books now teach six kingdoms since bacteria were split into two groups. Classifying life keeps improving!

briefs.competency: identify and explain evidence that current continents are separate parts of what was a single continent millions of years ago
existing_facts_en:
Could Mesosaurus swim across the Atlantic Ocean?

No! Mesosaurus was a coastal reptile that could not have crossed such a large ocean, so the continents must have been joined.

What evidence did Wegener use to support his theory?

He used matching coastlines, similar rock formations, identical fossils on separate continents, and climate clues like glacial deposits!
The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces — a clue they were once joined!
Matching fossils of animals and plants are found on separate continents, proving they were once connected!

Did all Philippine islands come from volcanoes?

Nope! Palawan was once part of Asia's big landmass and slowly drifted to its spot. That's why some Palawan animals look more like those in Borneo!
The matching shapes of coastlines prove continental drift! The east coast of South America and the west coast of Africa fit together perfectly like a jigsaw puzzle.

Why do we find the same ancient fossils on continents far apart?

Identical fossils of the same ancient plants and animals are found on far-apart continents, showing that these lands were once joined together!
Matching rock types, ages, and mountain ranges connect when separate continents are put back together, proving they were once one giant landmass!

briefs.competency: explore the school grounds or the local area to observe or collect different types of rocks, describing their similarities and differences in terms of features, such as texture, color, and grain crystal size
existing_facts_en: Galena is the main ore of lead! It appears as shiny gray cubic crystals and is very heavy for its size because lead is a dense metal.

Is all volcanic rock a crystal?

No! Obsidian is volcanic rock but not a crystal — it's amorphous (no crystal structure) because the molten rock cooled too fast. You can find it near volcanoes like Taal.
Fast-cooling lava makes tiny crystals, while magma cooling slowly underground makes big crystals like in granite!
You can't guess a mineral's hardness just by its color! Talc can be white, gray, or green, but it stays soft. Only a scratch test truly reveals its hardness.
Obsidian is a black glassy rock that forms when lava cools so rapidly that no crystals can grow. It is extremely sharp and was used by ancient people for tools and weapons!

What rock makes up most of the land beneath our feet?

Granite! It's the main rock of continental crust, made of quartz, feldspar, and mica, with large crystals and a white-to-gray speckled look.
Schist is a medium-to-high grade metamorphic rock with large visible crystals of mica and other minerals. The crystals line up in layers because pressure pushed from just one direction!

You can start identifying rocks by looking at three things: color, texture (smooth or rough?), and hardness (soft or hard — can you scratch it with a fingernail?). These are simple ways to begin learning about rocks!

Ever spotted tiny, layered rocks by the river?

Mudstone and siltstone are fine-grained sedimentary rocks! Mudstone has the tiniest clay particles, siltstone has silt grains. Both are gray or brown, found near rivers and road cuts!

briefs.competency: design and construct a simple electrical circuit to identify what materials will conduct electricity and use it to identify materials from the environment that will and will not conduct electricity
existing_facts_en: Insulators are materials that do not allow electricity to flow through them easily, and common examples include rubber, plastic, glass, wood, ceramic, paper, cloth, and dry soil.

Can pencil lead power a lightbulb?

Yes! Graphite, the material in pencil lead, is a non-metal that conducts electricity to power a small lightbulb when connected to a battery.

Why doesn't an insulator conduct electricity?

An insulator's electrons are tightly held in place, so they cannot move freely to carry electricity!

How can you test if a material is a conductor or insulator?

Use a simple circuit! If the material is a conductor, the bulb will light up to show it.
Rubber and plastic do not let electricity flow through! That is why they are used to cover wires safely.

Can a fruit really make electricity?

Yes! Test if something is a conductor by putting it in a circuit — if the bulb lights, current flows! Even a calamansi can make a little electricity using two different metals.

How can you test if something is a conductor or insulator?

Build a simple circuit with a battery and bulb! Put the object in — if the bulb lights up, it's a conductor! If it stays dark, it's an insulator!
Place an object in a circuit, and if the light turns on, it is a conductor! This means it lets electricity flow, just like metal.

Does all water conduct electricity?

Not really! Pure distilled water is an electrical insulator. It doesn't conduct electricity, unlike tap water with dissolved conductive minerals!

briefs.competency: investigate and describe the relationship among the projectile variables including the angle and velocity of release, and projectile height and range, using everyday activities such as shooting basketballs or kicking footballs
existing_facts_en: A monkey jumping from a branch at 38° with an initial velocity of 10 m/s follows the same projectile rules as any thrown object.
A soccer ball kicked at 35 m/s at a 20° angle is a projectile, and its height and range can be calculated with the same formulas.
The horizontal range of a projectile is calculated by multiplying its horizontal velocity component by the total time of flight.
As the launch angle increases from 20 degrees toward 45 degrees, the range of the projectile increases because the object stays in the air longer while still moving forward.
In projectile motion, forward and downward motions are independent! Your forward speed stays the same, while gravity only changes the downward motion.
With no air resistance and level ground, a thrown object travels the farthest (greatest range) when launched at an angle of 45 degrees!

What happens if you launch a projectile at two different angles that add up to 90 degrees, like 30 and 60?

They give the exact same range! But the steeper angle makes it go higher and stay in the air longer.

What determines how long a projectile stays in the air?

It depends only on its vertical motion (how high it goes up), not on how fast it moves forward!
A projectile reaches its highest point when its vertical speed becomes zero—it pauses for an instant before falling back down!

What happens to a projectile's range when you launch it faster at the same angle?

At the same angle, a faster launch speed means the projectile travels a greater range—it goes farther!

briefs.competency: distinguish between speed and velocity using the concept of vectors
existing_facts_en: Velocity is a measure of how fast an object moves and in what direction, so two objects with the same speed can have different velocities.

Why do we say a car’s speed is 60 km/h but its velocity is 60 km/h North?

Because speed is a scalar quantity that only tells you how fast, while velocity is a vector quantity that also tells you the direction!

What does it mean when a car’s velocity is 20 meters per second East?

The car's displacement changes by 20 meters every second, and it is moving toward the East!

Why can two runners have the same speed but different velocities?

Because they might run the same distance in the same time, but in different directions!

Why do we say a car's velocity is different from its speed?

Because velocity is speed with a direction! A car going 60 km/h north and another going 60 km/h south have the same speed but different velocities.

What exactly makes a quantity a vector or a scalar when we are studying motion?

Vectors like velocity, displacement, and force have size and direction. Scalars like speed and distance only have size, with no direction!
Speed only tells how fast something is going, but velocity also includes the direction it is moving!
Average speed and average velocity are different! Speed uses total distance, but velocity includes direction. If you return to your start, your velocity is zero, but your speed is not!

Are speed and velocity the same thing?

Speed tells you how fast. Velocity adds direction! '5 m/s' is speed, but '5 m/s heading north' is velocity.

What is the difference between speed and velocity?

Speed tells only how fast something moves, while velocity tells both how fast and in which direction it moves!

briefs.competency: explain that genetic information is passed on to offspring from both parents by the process of meiosis and fertilization
existing_facts_en:
Why are gametes haploid instead of diploid?

So that when a sperm and egg fuse during fertilization, the offspring gets the correct full set of 46 chromosomes, not double.

What is meiosis for?

Meiosis is a special cell division that produces sex cells, or gametes, like sperm and egg cells.

Will your child inherit your scars?

No! Only the DNA in egg and sperm passes to your children, so scars and tattoos on your body don't change that.
During meiosis, chromosomes can swap sections with each other, mixing genes into new combinations and creating more genetic variety.
In sexual reproduction, two parents each contribute genes, so their offspring carries a mix of traits from both.

Why isn't a child an exact copy of a parent?

Offspring look like their parents but are never exact copies — they get a mix of genes from both parents, making a combination unique to them.
When sex cells form, the two alleles separate so that only one gets passed on to the next generation.
When egg and sperm unite, the new cell ends up with two of each chromosome — one from the mother and one from the father.
For most traits, a child gets two alleles—one from mom and one from dad.
Half of your chromosomes come from your mother, and the other half come from your father.

briefs.competency: discuss the significant contributions of early scientists in the development of the periodic table
existing_facts_en: Not all elements fit Dobereiner's triad pattern, so scientists kept searching for a better way to organize them.

Who created the first periodic table?

Russian scientist Dmitri Mendeleev created the first widely used periodic table in 1869 by grouping elements with similar properties together.

How did Mendeleev predict new elements?

Mendeleev left empty gaps in his table and predicted what undiscovered elements would be like. When found, his predictions matched perfectly!
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian scientist who created the first widely used periodic table of the elements!

Who created the periodic table of elements back in 1869?

A Russian chemist named Dmitri Mendeleev created this awesome chart to organize all the elements!

How did Mendeleev know about undiscovered elements?

He left gaps in his periodic table and predicted elements like gallium and germanium!

Who discovered most of the noble gases like neon and xenon?

William Ramsay! He discovered neon, krypton, and xenon in 1898.

How did Mendeleev organize the elements?

He arranged the elements in order of increasing atomic mass and by their similar properties!

How did Mendeleev predict undiscovered elements?

He left gaps in his table and correctly predicted elements that had not yet been discovered!
Dmitri Mendeleev created the periodic table that neatly arranges all the elements by their properties! It helps us learn science.

briefs.competency: explain the advantage of high biodiversity in maintaining the stability of an ecosystem during difficult conditions, such as food shortages, disease, and climate change
existing_facts_en: High biodiversity means many different species live in one place, so when hard times come, some will likely survive and keep the ecosystem going.

Why is an ecosystem with high biodiversity better off?

With many different species, there are more food sources and helpers, so the ecosystem can survive changes and disasters more easily!

Why are fig trees called 'keystone'?

Fig trees are keystone species because they bear fruit even when nothing else in the forest is fruiting — so birds and bats always have food, even in lean times.
Biodiversity means the variety of living things in a place. The more varied the life, the more stable and healthy the ecosystem -- and the Philippines is one of the richest countries for it!
It's a myth that nothing happens when one species disappears. The effect is often slow — things seem fine at first, then the balance suddenly collapses later.

Why is a mixed forest healthier?

A forest is healthier when many kinds of trees grow together, not just one kind like ipil-ipil.
When cleaner fish disappear from a reef, parasites increase and the other fish become less healthy.

Why is having many animal species important?

Every animal has a role in nature -- some eat insects, some spread plant seeds. When there are many kinds and they're all connected, nature stays balanced and healthy.

Why is an ecosystem with many species tougher?

When many different species do the same job — like many kinds of insects that pollinate flowers — there's a backup if one disappears. That's why ecosystems with many species are more stable than ones with only a few!
Ecosystems with more kinds of species and more connected food webs recover better from disturbances than ecosystems with only a few species.

briefs.competency: discuss as a class how threats to biodiversity can lead to species extinction
existing_facts_en: Shark finning — cutting off a shark's fins and tossing the body back to sea — causes shark numbers to crash and hurts the coral reefs that depend on them.
When forests are cut down or animal homes are destroyed, animals lose their shelter and food — that's why many become endangered.
Because dugongs swim slowly, people can catch them easily — one reason these gentle animals are now in danger.
The tiny pilandok deer is endangered on Balabac island because of overhunting and the loss of its forest home.
The illegal wildlife trade shrinks the numbers of endangered animals like pangolins and tarsiers, making it even harder for them to recover in the wild.
The Philippine eagle is critically endangered from forest loss and hunting — that's why the law forbids anyone from shooting it.
The tamaraw is a Philippine buffalo found only in Mindoro. It grazes on grasses and plants, but sadly it's critically endangered from habitat loss and hunting.
The hawksbill sea turtle is critically endangered worldwide. For centuries, its beautiful shell (bekko or tortoiseshell) was harvested for jewelry, causing its numbers to drop dramatically.
Many cloud rats are now in danger, threatened by too much hunting and the loss of their forest homes.
Long ago, prairie dog towns were enormous — some stretched across the grassland almost as far as the eye could see. Today there are far fewer because much of their habitat was lost.

briefs.competency: identify the locations of major mountains, faults, volcanos, and ocean trenches using a map of the Philippine Archipelago, and interpret the features in relation to plate tectonics
existing_facts_en: The Philippine Trench is on the east, while the Manila Trench is on the west near the South China Sea. They are in different places and connect to different plates!

What connects to the Philippine Trench up north near Luzon?

The East Luzon Trough! Together, they form a long line of deep water on the east of our country.

Along the eastern edge of the Philippines lies the Philippine Trench—a super deep crack in the sea floor where one plate slides under another. That same motion builds the earthquakes, volcanoes, and islands!

The Manila Trench is a subduction zone west of the Philippines where the South China Sea floor dives under Luzon! It is a potential source of large earthquakes and tsunamis affecting the Luzon coastline!

Where can we find the Manila Trench?

It is found west of Luzon and Mindoro, right under the South China Sea!
You can find the Philippine Trench on the eastern side of our country, right inside the Pacific Ocean!

Where does the Philippine Fault run?

It runs all the way from northern Luzon, passes through Leyte, and goes down to southern Mindanao!
The Valley Fault System in Luzon is a huge geological fracture. This is where massive tectonic plates slowly grind past each other!
The Philippine Trench is a deep oceanic trench formed by the subduction of the Philippine Sea plate!
