What is the Philippine Trench and why is it dangerous?

The Philippine Trench is a deep underwater canyon in the Pacific Ocean where tectonic plates collide to create tsunami hazards.
The Ibalong Festival in Legazpi celebrates Mount Mayon! It's a perfect stratovolcano formed by tectonic plate subduction in the Pacific Ring of Fire.

briefs.competency: explain the difference between distance and displacement in everyday situations in relation to a reference point
existing_facts_en:
Can you travel a distance of 200 meters but still have zero displacement?

Yes! If you walk 100 meters East then 100 meters West, you return to your starting point. Your distance is 200 meters, but your displacement is zero because your initial and final positions are the same.

If I walk around the whole park, why is my distance so big even though I end up where I started?

Distance is the total length of the path you traveled, so every step you took around the park is counted, no matter which way you were facing.

Why is your displacement zero if you walk to a store and then walk back home?

Because displacement only cares about where you started and where you ended up, and those are the same spot!
On a grid where each box is 2 meters, you can count boxes to find distance along a path, but displacement is the straight-line count from start to end.
Distance is the total length of the path traveled, so every turn and curve along the way is counted.
A straight-line shortcut between two places represents displacement, because it shows only the shortest connection from start to finish.

A dog runs 10 m east, 5 m south, and 10 m west. How far did it travel?

It travelled 25 meters in distance, but its displacement is only 5 meters south from where it started!

If you walk 10 steps forward and 10 steps back, why is your distance 20 steps but your displacement zero?

Because distance counts every step you take, while displacement only looks at where you end up - and you end up exactly where you started!

Is it possible for your displacement to be zero even if you traveled a really long distance?

Yes! If an object returns to its exact starting point, its displacement is zero, even if the total distance traveled is large.
Average speed and average velocity are different! Speed uses total distance, but velocity includes direction. If you return to your start, your velocity is zero, but your speed is not!

What's the difference between distance and displacement?

Distance is the total path length you travel, while displacement is the straight-line gap from start to finish, plus its direction!

briefs.competency: explain the difference between heat and temperature
existing_facts_en:
Why does metal feel colder than wood in the same room?

They are actually at the exact same temperature, but the metal just feels colder to our hands!

Is a bigger ice cube actually colder than a small one?

Nope, both are exactly at 0°C! A bigger ice cube just takes longer to melt because it needs to absorb more heat, not because it is colder.
Metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature because it pulls heat away from your hand super fast — it is not actually colder, just a quick heat stealer!

What is the difference between heat and temperature?

Heat is energy moving from hot to cold objects. Temperature just measures the average motion energy of tiny particles inside!

What is the difference between heat and temperature?

Temperature measures how hot something is, while heat is the total thermal energy moving from one object to another!

What is the difference between heat and temperature?

Temperature measures how hot or cold something is! Heat is the energy that flows from a hotter object to a cooler one.
Heat and temperature are actually different! Heat is a form of energy, while temperature simply measures how hot something is.
A big pot of warm water holds more total heat than a small cup of hot water, even if the cup feels hotter!
Heat and temperature are different! Temperature measures how hot or cold a thing is, while heat (thermal energy) is the energy transferred from hot to cold.

Are temperature and heat the same thing?

Nope! Temperature measures average particle kinetic energy, while heat is the total energy transferred from one object to another.

What is the difference between temperature and heat in a bowl of hot soup?

Temperature measures the average speed of molecules in the soup, while heat is the total thermal energy transferred!

briefs.competency: differentiate plant and animal cells based on their organelles
existing_facts_en: Chloroplasts are found only in plant cells, and they make food from sunlight through photosynthesis.

How do animal and plant vacuoles differ?

Animal cells hold many small temporary vacuoles for food and waste, while plant cells have just one big permanent one!
Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts — animal cells don't have either!

Do animal cells have a cell wall?

No — which is why they are softer and often rounder in shape.

What do plant cells have that animal cells don't?

Three things! Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole — animal cells don't, but they have centrioles that help with cell division instead.

How is a plant cell different from an animal cell?

Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus, cell membrane, and cytoplasm—but a plant cell also has a stiff cell wall and chloroplasts for photosynthesis, which animal cells don't have.
A plant cell has a stiff cell wall and chloroplasts that an animal cell doesn't have — that's why the two look so different.

Why don't plant cells burst?

Plant cells have a tough wall made of cellulose. It keeps their shape strong and stops them from bursting even when they swell up with water.

What gives plant cells their shape?

A stiff outer layer called the cell wall wraps around each plant cell, giving it shape and support.
Plant cells usually have one large central vacuole full of water that helps keep the plant firm and upright.

What does the vacuole do in a plant cell?

Plant cells have a big central vacuole that stores water and helps keep the whole plant firm and standing upright.

briefs.competency: discuss how bodies of water and landforms affect typhoons
existing_facts_en: Warm Pacific Ocean water above 26°C fuels typhoons through evaporation! The warmer the water, the more energy for stronger typhoons.
A typhoon weakens after landfall because it loses the warm ocean water that gives it all its energy!
The Sierra Madre in eastern Luzon is the longest mountain range in the Philippines! It acts as a big shield against typhoons.
A storm surge is higher where the sea is shallow and the coast is flat, because the water piles up easily!

Did you know the Philippines has a giant shield made of mountains?

The Sierra Madre is the longest mountain range in the Philippines, running along eastern Luzon. It blocks strong storms from the Pacific Ocean, weakening winds before they reach our cities!
Most typhoons form in the Pacific Ocean and move west! Eastern islands like Samar and Bicol act as the first shield against these incoming storms.
When a typhoon hits land, it loses its warm water fuel and faces friction from the ground, causing it to weaken fast!

The Sierra Madre is the Philippines' longest mountain range! It acts as a barrier creating a 'rain shadow' effect, catching heavy typhoon rain in the east while keeping the Cagayan Valley drier and protected.
Typhoons form and gain strength only over warm ocean water, so they weaken quickly after hitting Philippine islands!
The Sierra Madre mountain range blocks many typhoons! Because of this, its eastern slopes get way more rain than inland areas.

Why does Eastern Samar get hit by storms first?

Because it faces the Pacific Ocean directly, it's the first Philippine landmass to feel incoming tropical cyclones!

briefs.competency: explain that the elements within a group in the periodic table have the same number of valence electrons
existing_facts_en:
Why are noble gases so special?

Noble gases like helium and neon are in the last column of the periodic table. They rarely react, so helium safely fills balloons and neon glows in signs!

Why do elements in the same group behave alike?

Because they have the same number of outer electrons! This controls exactly how they react with other things.
Noble gases like helium, neon, and argon almost never bond! Their outer shell is already full, so they don't need to gain or share electrons.
The vertical columns in the periodic table are called groups! Elements in the same group share similar properties.

Why do elements in the same group act alike?

Because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell!
In the periodic table, elements in the same group have the same valence electrons and similar chemical properties. For example, noble gases are almost unreactive!

What are the vertical columns of the periodic table called?

They are called groups! Elements found in the same group share very similar chemical properties.

Why do elements in the same main group behave similarly?

Because they have the exact same number of valence electrons! This makes them act alike in chemical reactions.
Halogens like fluorine and chlorine are in Group 17. They are reactive nonmetals that have exactly seven valence electrons!

Why are alkali metals like sodium and potassium so reactive in Group 1?

They are very reactive because they have just one valence electron!
Elements in a family behave alike because they share the same number of valence electrons, letting us predict their reactions!

briefs.competency: describe how seismic wave data has been used to develop a model for the internal structure and composition of the Earth
existing_facts_en:
How do scientists see deep inside the Earth?

Geologists use seismic waves from earthquakes! By watching how these waves bounce at layer boundaries, they map the deep structure inside the Earth.

How do scientists know Earth has a liquid outer core?

S waves (transverse seismic waves) cannot pass through liquid! After earthquakes, the absence of S waves in certain zones proved that Earth has a liquid outer core.

We can't drill all the way to the core! Scientists study seismic waves from earthquakes instead — as they pass through different layers, their speed and direction change, revealing Earth's hidden structure.
We can't see mantle convection — it's way too deep! But scientists use seismic waves from earthquakes to 'scan' inside the Earth and learn how it moves.

How do scientists study the mantle if they can't visit it?

Scientists study the mantle using earthquake (seismic) waves! These waves change speed and direction as they pass through Earth, revealing what's inside.
P-waves are fast compression waves that travel through anything. S-waves are slower shear waves that can't pass the liquid outer core. Their time gap tells the quake's distance!
We can't drill deep into the Earth, so scientists use earthquake seismic waves like an x-ray to see the layers inside!

How do scientists know the outer core is liquid?

S-waves cannot pass through liquid! Since they stop at the outer core, it proves the outer core is liquid.

What is the shadow zone inside the Earth?

The liquid outer core blocks and bends seismic waves, creating regions on the far side where no waves arrive!

How do scientists find the depth of Earth's boundaries?

When a seismic wave crosses into another layer, it changes speed and bends. Studying this bend reveals the boundary's depth!

What is the Moho boundary?

It's the boundary between the crust and mantle! It was discovered when seismic waves suddenly sped up passing through that level.

briefs.competency: gather information from secondary sources to identify ways to reduce the impact of collisions such as seatbelts, airbags, and crumple zones in vehicles
existing_facts_en: Seatbelts, airbags, and crumple zones in cars reduce collision impact by increasing the time over which your momentum changes.
A crumple zone is the part of a car designed to crush and fold in a crash! This makes the impact take longer, lowering the force on passengers.
In a crash, an airbag inflates fast to give your head and chest more time to stop, making the hitting force much smaller!
An airbag makes your body stop more slowly during a crash, so the push on you feels much softer and safer!
A seatbelt holds you in place when a car suddenly stops, keeping you safe from flying forward!
When a car crashes and stops suddenly, your body keeps its forward momentum! The seatbelt holds you tight, slowly reducing your momentum so you don't hit hard.
In a crash, your car stops suddenly, but your body wants to keep moving! The seatbelt applies a force to slow you down safely instead of throwing you forward. That's force changing motion!
Crumple zones in cars extend collision time! Since impulse equals force times time, a longer collision means less force hits the passengers — keeping them safer!

Why does a helmet protect your head in a bike crash?

The helmet's soft padding soaks up the crash's force so it doesn't hit your skull directly!

How does a seatbelt keep you safe during a crash?

It stops your body from flying forward because of inertia, keeping you safe and secure!

How do seatbelts keep us safe in a sudden car crash?

Seatbelts protect us by providing an unbalanced force to counteract our forward inertia during a sudden car crash!
Wearing a seatbelt applies a stopping force to your forward kinetic energy during a crash, preventing severe impact injuries!

briefs.competency: identify what proportion of the Earth's surface is covered with water as opposed to land
existing_facts_en: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water! That's exactly why our planet looks blue from space.

Why is Earth called the "blue planet"?

Because oceans cover more than half of it! About 7 out of 10 parts of Earth's surface are water.
Most meteorites splash into the ocean because water covers most of Earth's surface!
From space, Earth looks blue — that's why it's called the "blue planet"! Much of its surface is covered with oceans. Other planets look red, brown, or orange because they have no oceans.
Did you know the ocean is the main source of water vapor? That's because a huge 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water!

Why do we call Earth the "blue planet"?

About three-quarters of Earth's surface is covered by water! That huge amount of water is exactly why our home is called the "blue planet"!
About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water! That is why we call it the Blue Planet.

How much of Earth is actually land?

Only about 29% of Earth's surface is land! The rest of the surface is water.
The ocean covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface, which is way more than the land!
Wow, about 71 percent of Earth's surface is covered by water!

How much of Earth is actually dry land?

Only about 29 percent of Earth's surface is land—the rest is water!
Oceans cover about 71% of Earth's surface and hold roughly 97% of all the water on our entire planet!

briefs.competency: relate the shape of a volcano's cone to its composition
existing_facts_en: Shield volcanoes are tall and broad with gentle slopes, formed by low-viscosity basaltic lava that flows easily and spreads over large distances.
Volcanoes differ! Some erupt gently with runny lava, while others explode violently with thick lava and ash. Mayon Volcano is famous for its perfect cone shape!
Thin runny lava flows far easily, while thick sticky lava moves slowly and often causes more explosive eruptions!
Some volcanoes are broad and gently sloped like a shield, while others are steep cones, depending on the kind of lava!

Why are shield volcanoes so wide and flat?

Their basaltic lava is very fluid (low viscosity) and flows far before cooling, giving them wide, gentle slopes. Unlike Philippine stratovolcanoes, they don't erupt explosively!

Why do Philippine volcanoes like Mayon erupt so explosively?

Most Philippine volcanoes are stratovolcanoes (composite cones) with steep sides made of alternating layers of lava and pyroclastic material. Their thick, viscous lava traps gases, causing very explosive eruptions!
A cinder cone is the smallest volcano type, built from cinders and scoria thrown out of a single vent! It forms quickly, and its activity usually ends within months to years.
A stratovolcano is a tall, steep cone built from alternating layers of lava and ash!

Why does Mayon have a perfect cone shape?

Because layers of lava and ash pile up evenly into a steep cone!

Why is a shield volcano low and broad?

A shield volcano is low and broad because its runny lava flows far before it cools and hardens!
Mayon Volcano in Albay is a perfect cone stratovolcano that frequently erupts, producing fast-moving pyroclastic flows of hot gas and rock!
Shield volcanoes like Mauna Loa erupt gently! They ooze thin, fluid basaltic lava that flows slowly downhill instead of exploding.

briefs.competency: draw the structure of an atom in terms of the nucleus and electron shells
existing_facts_en:
How do electrons move around the nucleus?

Electrons move quickly around the outside of the nucleus, arranged in layers or shells surrounding it!
Electrons are neatly arranged in special levels or shells all around the center nucleus!

How is an atom built in the Bohr model?

It has a tiny center nucleus of protons and neutrons! Electrons orbit around it in fixed energy levels or shells.
Atoms are tiny, but they have even smaller parts! Inside are protons and neutrons in the center nucleus, with electrons moving around the outside.
Even though atoms are super tiny, most of an atom is actually empty space! The nucleus in the middle is extremely small, and electrons orbit far, far away from it.
An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus with protons and neutrons, surrounded by an electron cloud. Amazingly, more than 99.9% of its volume is just empty space!

How do electrons move in Niels Bohr's model?

Niels Bohr made a model where electrons orbit the nucleus just like planets around the sun!
Bohr said electrons travel in fixed paths! They orbit in specific energy levels around the nucleus.

How do electrons move around the nucleus?

In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a model where electrons orbit the nucleus just like planets!
An atom's electrons are arranged in shells, or energy levels, around the nucleus. The farther a shell is from the nucleus, the higher its energy level!
Ernest Rutherford fired tiny particles at thin gold foil and discovered a small, dense, positive nucleus hiding right at the center of the atom!
Niels Bohr improved the atomic model! He showed that electrons orbit the nucleus in specific energy levels, and never just sit in between!

briefs.competency: describe the types of plate boundaries found around the Earth
existing_facts_en: There are three types of convergent plate interactions: oceanic-continental, oceanic-oceanic, and continental-continental, each forming different landforms.
When spreading continues at a divergent boundary, the crust may break into segments and form a rift valley, which can grow into a linear sea like the Red Sea.
As plates pull away from each other, a vertical space called a rift valley is created.
Ocean trenches form where two tectonic plates crash together and one dives beneath the other!

How does new ocean floor get made?

At mid-ocean ridges, plates pull apart! The mantle rises up, partly melts, and creates brand-new crust on the ocean floor.

Where is the longest mountain range on Earth?

It's under the ocean! The mid-ocean ridge stretches thousands of kilometers along the sea floor, forming where plates pull apart and lava hardens into new rock.

What happens when tectonic plates just slide past each other?

At a transform fault boundary, two plates slide horizontally past each other! No new land is created or sinks, creating large earthquakes but no volcanoes. The Philippine Fault is a transform fault!

There are three plate boundaries: convergent — plates collide and one subducts or land crunches up; divergent — plates move apart and new crust forms; transform — plates slide horizontally past each other with no crust created or destroyed.
At a divergent boundary, two plates pull apart! Magma rises from below, cools down, and forms brand new crust.

What happens when plates crash into each other?

At a convergent boundary, plates push and collide! This creates tall mountains, deep trenches, and lots of earthquakes and volcanoes.
At a transform boundary, plates slide and grind past each other sideways! This rough rubbing often causes strong earthquakes.
When a continental plate starts to split, a deep rift valley forms — like the East African Rift! Over time, water fills it and creates a brand-new ocean.

briefs.competency: describe how fossils can be used for dating the age of rocks and sediments
existing_facts_en: Fossils in higher, newer rock layers usually look like species alive today, while fossils in deeper, older layers are often very different.
Thousands of layers of sedimentary rock full of fossils give us evidence of the very long history of changing life on Earth.
Fossils show how living things changed over time — older fossils lie in deeper rock layers, while newer ones are found closer to the surface.
In layered rock, fossils buried deeper are usually older than those near the top — so scientists read the layers to learn the order living things appeared on Earth.

Why do scientists look at deeper rock layers for older fossils?

Usually, fossils in deeper rock layers are older than those above them! This helps us see the order living things appeared.

How do some fossils help tell the age of rocks?

Fossils that were widespread but lived only for a short time are used as markers to tell the age of the rock they are found in!

How can rocks tell us which fossils are older?

In undisturbed rock layers, the fossils at the bottom are older, while the ones near the top are younger!
Index fossils are easy to identify, widespread, and lived for a short time! Geologists use them like time markers to match the age of rocks worldwide!

What are ammonites?

Ammonites were extinct cephalopods with coiled shells, like squid relatives! They were so diverse and widespread that scientists use them as index fossils to date Mesozoic rocks. All ammonites died out with the asteroid impact 66 million years ago.
Scientists know what lived in each era by studying fossils! These are found in different layers of rock.

How do scientists learn about ancient life?

They study fossils found in rock layers to discover what life existed and how old those layers are!

How do index fossils help scientists?

An index fossil comes from a widespread organism that lived for a short time. It acts as a guide to determine the age of its rock layer!

briefs.competency: identify that momentum is conserved before and after the collision of objects
existing_facts_en: In every collision, the total momentum before impact equals the total momentum after impact, even when kinetic energy is lost.

What happens to momentum when objects crash?

It never disappears! In a collision, total momentum stays the same. It just transfers from one object to another.

What happens to momentum when objects collide?

In a collision with no outside force, total momentum before equals total momentum after! It's never lost, only shared around!
In an inelastic collision, objects stick together or get dented, turning some motion energy into heat and sound, but total momentum is still conserved!
When a cannon fires, the cannonball flies forward while the cannon pushes back, because the total momentum must always stay balanced!

How does a rocket fly up into space?

It blasts hot gas downward very fast! By conservation of momentum, this pushes the rocket itself upward!
In a Newton's cradle, releasing one steel ball at the end makes just one ball fly out the far end because momentum and motion energy pass through elastic collisions!

What happens when two objects with equal momentum but opposite directions collide and stick together?

Their momenta can cancel each other out, and they both stop completely!

What happens to the total momentum of objects during a collision?

The total momentum of the objects before is exactly equal to the total momentum after!
In a Newton's cradle, when one ball hits the row, the momentum travels through the middle balls and the last ball swings out!

Why does a gun kick backward when it fires?

When a gun fires, the bullet zooms forward and the gun kicks backward — because total momentum must always stay balanced!
In a closed system, total momentum before and after a collision stays exactly the same! This important physics rule is called the conservation of momentum.
In any collision, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after! This is called conservation of momentum, just like when billiard balls collide.

briefs.competency: describe important types of chemical reactions (combination, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement)
existing_facts_en: In a double replacement reaction, two compounds exchange ions with each other, like magnesium oxide and calcium sulfide swapping partners to form calcium oxide and magnesium sulfide.
Water can be broken down into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas by passing direct electricity through it, a process called electrolysis.
Nitrogen alone isn't enough to make nitrogen oxides -- oxygen is needed too. When lightning strikes, its heat pushes the air's nitrogen and oxygen together to combine and form them.

What happens in a single replacement reaction?

A more reactive element takes the place of another in a compound, like iron displacing copper!
In a synthesis or combination reaction, two or more substances join to form a single new compound. For example, hydrogen and oxygen form water!
In electrolysis, electric current passes through water to split it into two gases: hydrogen at one electrode and oxygen at the other!
In a decomposition reaction, one compound breaks apart into simpler substances! For example, electricity can split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Decomposition is a chemical change where bacteria break down dead leaves into nutrient-rich soil during composting!
In a combination or synthesis reaction, two or more substances join together to form a single new product, like hydrogen and oxygen forming water!
In a decomposition reaction, a single substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances, which is often caused by heat or electricity!
In a single replacement reaction, one element takes the place of another in a compound, like a more active metal replacing a less active one!

What happens in a double replacement reaction?

Two compounds exchange their parts, called ions, to form two new compounds, and it often produces a solid precipitate!
When an acid reacts with many metals, hydrogen gas comes out as fun bubbles! A dissolved salt is left behind in the water.

briefs.competency: observe and describe the difference between living and non-living things and give examples of each that can be found in the local environment
existing_facts_en:
Is coral a rock or something alive?

Surprise — coral is actually a living animal, not a rock, even though it feels hard like one!

How do you know something is living?

Living things grow, take in food or energy, breathe, respond to their surroundings, and reproduce — rocks and water don't do any of these.

Is coral a rock or a plant?

Neither! Coral is actually made of tiny living animals called polyps.

Are pond microbes actually alive?

Those tiny things in pond water aren't just dirt — pond microbes are truly alive because they eat, move, and reproduce like other living things.

Is yeast actually alive?

Yes! It's a tiny living fungus made of just one cell — that's why it needs to eat and grow, unlike a plain powder.

Is the green stuff on a pond just trash?

No! That green floating stuff is actually a living plant with leaves and roots, making its own food from sunlight just like other plants!
Yeast and baking soda both make dough rise, but differently: yeast is alive and needs sugar and time, while baking soda is a fast-acting chemical.

Is coral a rock, a plant, or something else?

Coral is neither! It's made of thousands of tiny animals called polyps. Each one builds a hard skeleton, and together they form a whole reef.

Is coral a rock?

No -- coral is a living animal! Each tiny polyp has a mouth and tentacles to catch food; the hard part is just the house it builds around itself.

Why does a virus need another living cell?

A virus has no parts for eating, growing, or making its own energy, so it must use another living thing's cell to survive.
A rocky reef is just dead stone, but a coral reef is built by living animals that keep growing and adding new skeleton — so it can heal and spread, unlike plain rock.
Even if a stalactite 'grows,' it’s not alive like a plant! It’s just rock getting bigger as mineral layers pile up. It doesn't eat or breathe.

Is soil just dead dirt?

Nope! Healthy soil is packed with millions of living organisms like earthworms and bacteria!

briefs.competency: describe uniform velocity and represent it using distance-time graphs
existing_facts_en: On a distance-time graph, a straight line shows constant speed, but a curve getting steeper means the object is speeding up or accelerating!
On a distance-time graph, a flat line means the object is at rest and not moving!
On a distance-time graph, the slope shows your average speed! A steeper line means you're going faster, while a flat line means you've stopped moving.
To get speed from a distance-time graph, divide the line's rise (distance) by its sideways run (time). That ratio is the slope, which is exactly the speed!
A downward line on a distance-time graph doesn't mean time goes backward! It means the object is moving back to its start, so its distance shrinks.
Distance-time and speed-time graphs are different! In distance-time, height is distance and slope is speed. In speed-time, height is speed, and a flat line means constant speed!
Think highest means fastest on a distance-time graph? Nope! Speed comes from the STEEPNESS of the line, not height. A high but flat line means you actually stopped!
Want the average speed of a whole trip? Just draw a straight line from the first point to the last point! The slope of that line is your average speed.

What do parallel lines on a distance-time graph tell us?

Parallel lines mean both objects move at the same speed! One might have left earlier, but they travel at one equal speed — they just never meet.
Why does a straight line mean constant speed? Because the object adds the same distance every second — equal upward steps mean no curve, just a perfectly straight line!
On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means a faster object! A flat line means it's stopped. You can easily see the speed just by looking at the line's steepness.
On a distance-time graph, a steadily rising line shows a moving object. The steeper the line goes up, the faster its motion!
On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means faster motion, while a flat line means the object is standing still!

briefs.competency: use examples of food pyramids to describe the transfer of energy between organisms from one trophic level to another
existing_facts_en: Biomass is the total mass of organic molecules minus water in an organism, and it decreases as you go up each trophic level.
Only about 10% of the energy at one feeding level passes to the next; the rest is used up for breathing and moving, or lost as heat.
At each step of a food chain, a lot of energy is lost as heat — so less and less gets passed on to the next animal.
In the ocean, tiny plankton form the huge base of the food pyramid, while sharks at the very top are far fewer in number.

Why is an energy pyramid pyramid-shaped?

An energy pyramid is wide at the bottom, where producers are, and narrow at the top, because energy is lost at each level of the food chain.

Why are there so few top predators?

Less and less energy reaches each higher level of a food chain, so only a few big predators can be supported at the very top.

Why is the top of an energy pyramid always smallest?

It measures how much energy is stored at each level — and that's exactly why the top level is always the tiniest!
There are so many plants at the base of the food pyramid because they're the starting source of energy for every other living thing.
At each level of a food chain, energy shrinks because animals use it to move and breathe, and much escapes as heat — that's why only a few big predators reach the top.

Why are there fewer predators than plants?

It's not just luck — predators are few and plants are many because energy is lost at every level of the food chain.

Why are there fewer predators than plants?

There are usually fewer predators at the top of the food chain than plants at the bottom, because energy gets smaller and smaller as it moves up.
Energy doesn't get recycled back through the food pyramid -- fresh energy from the sun must keep arriving.

Why are there so few big predators?

Only a little energy is left at the top of the food pyramid, so there's barely enough to support large predators — that's why there are so few!

briefs.competency: recognize that scientists use models to explain phenomena that cannot be easily seen or detected
existing_facts_en:
How do toy volcanoes erupt with foam?

They use baking soda and vinegar to overflow with foam and look like they are erupting!
The atom model changed over time! It went from Dalton's solid ball, to Thomson's 'raisin bread', to Rutherford's nucleus, and finally Bohr's orbiting-electron model.
A molecule model uses balls and sticks to show how atoms join together through bonds to form a cool molecule!

How does soap wash away grease?

In oily water, soap molecules form micelles! These are spherical clusters that trap grease in the center and use water-loving ends on the outside to wash it all away.

How do electrons move in Niels Bohr's model?

Niels Bohr made a model where electrons orbit the nucleus just like planets around the sun!

How do electrons move around the nucleus?

In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a model where electrons orbit the nucleus just like planets!
Niels Bohr created the famous Bohr model of the atom in 1913! It shows electrons orbiting the nucleus like planets around the sun.

How can we picture electrical current?

Think of water in a pipe! The wire is the pipe, and current is the water flowing inside. A stronger flow means more current, just like more water passing through!
Scientists use the ray model of light! They draw straight arrows to show the exact direction that light travels.
Light behaves as both a wave and as tiny energy packets called photons! Scientists use both models together to explain how light works.
Scientists use computer climate models tested against past climate to predict the future! These show temperatures will keep rising depending on how much greenhouse gas humans add.

How do scientists show what type of rock is hiding under the ground?

They use a geologic map! Different colors and symbols show the type and age of rocks, made here by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB).

What is a globe?

A globe is a small, round model of Earth showing its ball shape and where lands and oceans are!

briefs.competency: describe the different types of volcanoes found around the world according to their: a. activity b. type of eruption c. location in the crust
existing_facts_en: Volcanoes come in three types: active ones like Taal and Mayon that erupt or may erupt again, dormant ones sleeping quietly but able to wake, and extinct ones unlikely to ever erupt.
Volcanoes differ! Some erupt gently with runny lava, while others explode violently with thick lava and ash. Mayon Volcano is famous for its perfect cone shape!

What are the three kinds of volcanoes?

Active — erupted recently or could soon. Dormant — sleeping for a long time but might wake up. Extinct — not expected to erupt again. PHIVOLCS studies which kind each volcano is!
A volcano is active if it may erupt, dormant if it's been quiet a long time, and extinct if it will never erupt again!

What are the three types of volcanoes?

Volcanoes can be active (able to erupt), dormant (sleeping but able to wake up), or extinct (not expected to ever erupt again)!

What makes a volcano "active"?

An active volcano erupted recently or could erupt again anytime! It is still "alive" inside because hot magma is moving beneath it.

Why do Philippine volcanoes like Mayon erupt so explosively?

Most Philippine volcanoes are stratovolcanoes (composite cones) with steep sides made of alternating layers of lava and pyroclastic material. Their thick, viscous lava traps gases, causing very explosive eruptions!
A cinder cone is the smallest volcano type, built from cinders and scoria thrown out of a single vent! It forms quickly, and its activity usually ends within months to years.

Why do stratovolcanoes erupt so violently and explosively?

It is because their lava is very thick and sticky! This makes their eruptions super explosive.
Mayon Volcano in Albay is a perfect cone stratovolcano that frequently erupts, producing fast-moving pyroclastic flows of hot gas and rock!
Mayon Volcano in Albay is a classic stratovolcano formed by many layers of hardened lava and ash!
During the explosive eruption stage of a volcano, high-pressure magma blasts ash and rock fragments high into the atmosphere!
When trapped volcanic gases expand rapidly, a stratovolcano's explosive eruption stage shatters the magma and blasts ash and pumice into the atmosphere!

briefs.competency: using information from secondary sources identify the different parts of the cell where photosynthesis and respiration occur
existing_facts_en: Chloroplasts are found only in plant cells, and they make food from sunlight through photosynthesis.

What gives plants their green color?

Chlorophyll is the green substance inside chloroplasts that captures sunlight and gives plants their green color!
Plant cells have chloroplasts that make food using sunlight!

Where does photosynthesis happen?

Photosynthesis mostly happens in a plant's leaves, inside tiny cell parts called chloroplasts.
The palisade mesophyll is a layer of cells near the top of a leaf packed with chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

Why is the mitochondrion called the cell's 'powerhouse'?

They make the energy the cell uses from food.
In the light reactions of photosynthesis, chloroplasts use sunlight to split water apart, releasing oxygen and making ATP energy.
Inside every leaf, tiny green parts called chloroplasts turn sunlight, water, and air into the plant's food.

Where does photosynthesis happen inside a leaf?

Inside tiny parts of leaf cells called chloroplasts! That's where the chlorophyll is, and where photosynthesis takes place.
Plant cells do two jobs: photosynthesis in the chloroplasts, using sunlight to make food, and cellular respiration in the mitochondria, using that food to release energy.
The mitochondria makes energy from food inside the cell — that's exactly why it's nicknamed the cell's powerhouse.
Inside leaf cells are tiny green parts called chloroplasts! This is where photosynthesis happens and oxygen is made. The chlorophyll inside them absorbs the sun's light to get started.
Oxygen doesn't come from the soil or roots! It is made in the LEAVES inside chloroplasts. Roots only take in water and minerals, not oxygen for us.

briefs.competency: develop a timeline for the historical background of the development of the current Atomic Model that identifies tiny particles as atoms
existing_facts_en: The atom model changed over time! It went from Dalton's solid ball, to Thomson's 'raisin bread', to Rutherford's nucleus, and finally Bohr's orbiting-electron model.
John Dalton proposed the modern atomic theory, stating that all matter is made of tiny atoms!

Who discovered the nucleus, the dense center of the atom?

Ernest Rutherford discovered the nucleus, the dense center of the atom!
Rutherford discovered the nucleus using the gold foil experiment! He fired tiny particles at a super thin sheet of gold.
Democritus, an ancient Greek philosopher, first thought of the idea that everything is made of tiny atoms!
Dalton believed the atom was the smallest piece of matter. He thought it could not be divided further!
Did you know J.J. Thomson discovered the tiny electron way back in 1897? He was the very first scientist to find it!
The amazing electron was officially discovered in the year 1897! It was a huge step in understanding what makes up everything around us.
Ernest Rutherford is the famous scientist credited with discovering the proton in 1919! He helped us understand the positive parts of atoms.

Who first imagined the atom?

Democritus, an ancient Greek, first imagined the 'atom'! He named it meaning 'uncuttable' because he thought it couldn't be split.

Who created the 'plum pudding model' of the atom in 1904?

J.J. Thomson created it in 1904.

Who put the nucleus at the center of the atom model?

Ernest Rutherford, in his nuclear model of 1911.
In the early 1800s, John Dalton said all matter is made of tiny, unbreakable atoms! Atoms of one element are twins, but different from other elements.

briefs.competency: describe electromagnetic radiation (EMR) as energy that is created by the vibrations of electrically charged particles which allows it to travel through materials or space as transverse waves
existing_facts_en: Electromagnetic waves carry energy called radiation, which is why they are also known as electromagnetic radiation.
A radio wave is an electromagnetic wave made of vibrating electric and magnetic fields—not sound! It's in the same family as light and can travel through the empty vacuum of space.
To make a radio wave, a transmitter pushes electrons back and forth in a metal antenna. This wiggling sends out the wave! At the other end, the wave wiggles electrons in the receiver's antenna.
The Sun's heat reaches Earth by radiation! These electromagnetic waves, mainly infrared, need no medium and can easily cross the vacuum of space.

How do polarized sunglasses reduce glare?

Normal light vibrates in all directions. Polarized sunglasses only let light vibrating in one direction pass through, blocking glare from smooth surfaces!
Radiant energy from the Sun travels through the empty vacuum of space without needing any physical matter at all!
Did you know? Light waves can travel through the empty vacuum of outer space without needing any physical medium!
Sunlight reaches Earth as an electromagnetic wave through the empty vacuum of space, meaning light does not need air to move!
Sunlight travels through the empty vacuum of outer space to reach Earth! Light doesn't need a physical medium to travel.
The Sun warms your skin through radiation! It sends invisible infrared waves right through the empty vacuum of space to reach you.
Unlike sound, light waves don't need air or any physical medium to travel through the empty vacuum of space!
Unlike sound, an electromagnetic wave needs no medium! It travels right through the vacuum of space, which is why light from the Sun and stars reaches us.
Electromagnetic waves are produced when an electric charge changes its motion or speeds up! This happens when electrons vibrate back and forth inside an antenna.

briefs.competency: describe how high voltage electricity from power plants is generated and safely distributed to industries, businesses, and homes, including the role of substations (grid stations), and electric meters
existing_facts_en:
Why is electricity sent at very high voltage over long distances?

High-voltage transmission keeps the current low, and since power loss is P = I²R, lower current means much less energy is wasted as heat in the wires.
A transformer changes the voltage of electricity—raising it for long travel and lowering it before it reaches your home!

What happens to electricity at a substation?

At a substation, the high voltage is lowered before electricity is sent to homes in the area!
From the substation, electricity travels along poles on the street and right into our homes!
Your home's electric meter measures exactly how much electricity your family uses, counting it all up in kilowatt-hours!
Almost all the electricity in our homes comes from large generators in power plants that are spun by turbines!
Before reaching faraway cities, electricity passes through a transformer! It raises the voltage so power can travel long distances on lines without large losses.
The electric meter measures energy in kilowatt-hours (kWh)! One kWh means using a 1,000-watt appliance for one hour. Your electricity bill is based on the kWh you consume.
Move a magnet in and out of a wire coil and a galvanometer shows current — this is electromagnetic induction, the principle behind all generators.
Those small transformers on Philippine utility poles step down voltage — they convert 13,000 volts from the distribution line to safe 220 volts for our homes!
A transformer's primary (N1) to secondary (N2) coil turns ratio sets the voltage ratio (V1/V2 = N1/N2)! For example, 100 primary and 10 secondary turns reduces voltage 10 times.

Ever wonder how your electric bill is calculated?

A home electric meter measures your energy use in kilowatt-hours, and that exact number is what your electric bill is based on!

How does a power plant make electricity from coal?

Coal is burned to heat water into powerful steam! This steam spins a turbine, and the turbine generates electricity for our homes.

How do power plants make electricity from fossil fuels?

They burn fossil fuel to boil water into steam! The steam spins a turbine connected to a generator, and boom — electricity flows to your home!

briefs.competency: compare the life cycles of mammals from birth to adulthood, birds from egg to a mature organism, and plants from seed to a young plant, and then to a mature plant
existing_facts_en:
Is rice harvested right after planting?

No! Rice must be cared for several months with water, sunshine, and nutrients before it flowers and forms grains ready to harvest.
When a jackfruit seed sprouts, a root comes out first and grows down into the soil, then a shoot pushes up toward the sun.
When a seed germinates, the root grows down first, then the shoot grows up, until the seedling opens its very first leaves!
When the soil is wet and warm, a rice seed sprouts and grows into a small seedling.
A seed doesn't have to sprout right away — it can rest quietly in the soil for a long time, waiting for just the right conditions.
Before its first leaves appear, a seedling uses the food stored inside the seed as its starting energy.
A seed can rest for a long time, waiting until there's enough water and warmth before it finally sprouts.
A seed can be 'dormant,' alive but waiting, until it gets enough water, warmth, and air—then it turns 'active' and sprouts a root and shoot!
The life cycle of Philippine rice, or palay, starts as a tiny seed, grows into a plant, and finally produces grain-filled panicles ready for harvest!
Most plants start as a seed, sprout roots and leaves, then flower and make fruit with new seeds to start the cycle again.
From one planted kernel, a corn plant grows, its tassel and silk appear, and finally a new ear full of kernels forms that can be planted again.
During germination, a mung bean seed soaks up water, and its radicle pushes out to become the very first root.

What do we call a young sprouting plant?

A young plant that just sprouted from a seed is called a seedling.
When a seed starts to grow, the root is the very first part to poke out, so it can search for water in the soil.

briefs.competency: observe and describe examples of accelerating objects at school and in the local community, including objects that show uniform circular motion
existing_facts_en: In uniform circular motion, an object moves around a circle at a constant speed, but its direction keeps changing at every moment!

Does centripetal force change how fast an object moves?

No! Centripetal force changes only the direction of motion, not the speed. That is why speed stays the same in uniform circular motion!
Even at constant speed, an object in circular motion has an acceleration pointing toward the center because its velocity direction keeps changing!
Tilted road curves help cars turn safely! The tilt adds extra centripetal force pushing toward the center of the curve.
Spinning doesn't push you outward! Your body wants to go straight, but the turning pulls you inward—making it feel like you're pushed out.

Why do you need to hold on tighter on a fast merry-go-round?

The faster a merry-go-round turns, the stronger you feel thrown off! You must hold on tighter so you don't slide away from the center.

How does a ferris wheel at the fair move its riders?

It is a large wheel that turns in a circle! Riders go up and down as they move around it.
If you spin a bucket of water fast in a circle, it won't spill! The circular motion keeps pressing the water against the bottom.

Why doesn't water spill when you swing a bucket in a circle?

A force called centripetal force pulls the bucket toward the center! This keeps the water inside, even when the bucket is upside down at the very top.
A satellite doesn't fall to Earth because it moves so fast sideways! As gravity pulls it down, it keeps missing the Earth's curve and circles around instead.
The Diwata-2 microsatellite orbits Earth in continuous freefall, experiencing microgravity while zooming at roughly 27,000 kilometers per hour!

Why do motorcycle riders lean when turning?

They lean into the turn to stay perfectly balanced against the force pushing them outward!

How does the Moon stay in orbit?

In orbital motion, the gravitational step is Earth's pull acting as a centripetal force to curve the Moon's path!

How does a satellite stay in orbit around Earth?

It is constantly falling toward Earth! But it moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing the ground.

briefs.competency: describe how relative and absolute dating techniques are used to determine the subdivisions of geologic time
existing_facts_en:
How do scientists know a fossil's real age?

Through isotopic (radioactive) dating, they measure the actual age of fossils and rocks in millions of years — proof that enough time passed for life to slowly change.
Scientists use radioactive decay to find the age of old things! Carbon-14 in bones and wood slowly decays. By measuring what's left, they know how old a fossil is.

How do we know the age of old fossils?

Scientists use carbon-14 to find the age of old remains and fossils in a process called carbon dating!
Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope that decays at a known rate! By measuring how much remains in an ancient organic sample, scientists can tell how long ago the organism died.

Why do scientists look at deeper rock layers for older fossils?

Usually, fossils in deeper rock layers are older than those above them! This helps us see the order living things appeared.
The bottom rock layer is the oldest—it was laid down first. The top layer is the youngest. This simple rule is called the law of superposition.
If a crack or hardened lava cuts across many rock layers, it is younger than those layers! The layers had to be there first to be cut. This is called cross-cutting!
When a volcano erupts, its ash spreads wide and falls all at once, making a thin layer of the exact same age everywhere! It is an excellent time marker, like the 1991 Mount Pinatubo ash!

How do scientists read time in lake mud?

They count varves! These are annual sediment layers: a thick coarse layer from spring or summer, and a thin fine layer from winter. Each pair equals one year of deposits.
Scientists discover a rock's age using radioactive dating, which measures the decay of radioactive elements inside the rock!
In an undisturbed stack of rock layers, the oldest layer sits at the bottom and the youngest is on top — that's the law of superposition!

How do scientists find the exact age of a rock?

Through absolute dating! Scientists measure the radioactive isotopes left in a rock to calculate its actual age in years.

How do rocks tell time?

A half-life is the time for half a radioactive isotope to decay. Since this rate is constant, it acts as a natural clock to measure rock age!
Scientists estimate Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, based on radiometric dating of the oldest known meteorites and moon rocks!

briefs.competency: demonstrate in practical situations and describe that acceleration is a change in speed and/or direction as the result of a net force
existing_facts_en: A falling fruit accelerates downward because the unbalanced force of gravity acts on it, changing its state of motion.

If you throw a ball upward at 30 m/s, how fast is it moving just before you catch it?

It is moving at 30 m/s again, but now downward, so its velocity is negative 30 m/s!
An object's acceleration is always in the direction of the net force! A forward net force speeds it up, backward slows it down, and sideways makes it turn.
When something slows down, it still has acceleration! The force points opposite to its motion, called deceleration or negative acceleration.

Does centripetal force change how fast an object moves?

No! Centripetal force changes only the direction of motion, not the speed. That is why speed stays the same in uniform circular motion!
Even at constant speed, an object in circular motion has an acceleration pointing toward the center because its velocity direction keeps changing!

Who wins in a game of tug-of-war?

The side that pulls with greater force wins and drags the other side!
A paddle can also steer! Paddle only on the right side and the boat turns left. Paddle only on the left and it turns right. You can even use the blade like a rudder!

What happens when fishermen use a stronger pulling force on the heavy net?

The stronger the pulling force, the faster the heavy net moves toward them!
In physics, acceleration means ANY change in speed OR direction! A force can speed up, slow down, or turn an object. Even a car turning at constant speed is accelerating!

Does the direction you push matter?

Yes! The direction of a force changes the result. Push the same way it's going — it speeds up. Push against it — it slows down. Push from the side — it turns!

Is a car accelerating when it turns?

Yes! Acceleration is any change in speed or direction. So a car speeding up, slowing down, or turning a corner is all accelerating!

Why do motorcycle riders lean when turning?

They lean into the turn to stay perfectly balanced against the force pushing them outward!

What makes a falling apple speed up?

Acceleration is the free fall stage where Earth's gravity constantly increases the apple's downward speed!

briefs.competency: write the chemical formula and chemical names of some common ionic compounds, including sodium chloride (NaCl), magnesium oxide (MgO), potassium chloride (KCl) and magnesium chloride (MgCl2)
existing_facts_en: To write an ionic formula, use the crisscross method: switch the oxidation numbers of the positive and negative ions to become subscripts.

How do we name a simple ionic compound?

The metal's name comes first, followed by the nonmetal ending in '-ide'! For example, we call it sodium chloride.

Why does MgCl2 need TWO chlorines for one magnesium?

Magnesium has a +2 charge, but chlorine is only -1. So you need TWO chlorines (-1 and -1) to balance the +2 charge. That makes MgCl2!
Unlike sodium which is always +1, transition metals can have more than one charge! Iron can be Fe2+ or Fe3+, so we see iron(II) and iron(III) in compound names.

What is the chemical formula for table salt?

It is NaCl, or sodium chloride! It is an ionic compound made of sodium (Na+) and chloride (Cl-) ions held together by opposite electrical charges.

What is the chemical formula of table salt?

The chemical formula of table salt is NaCl!
The chemical formula of baking soda, also known as sodium bicarbonate, is NaHCO3!

What is the chemical formula for rust?

The chemical formula of rust, also known as iron oxide, is Fe2O3!
The chemical formula for the table salt you use is NaCl, which stands for sodium and chlorine!
The halogen chlorine joins with sodium to make sodium chloride (NaCl) — that's your everyday table salt!

What is the chemical formula for the table salt we use every day?

The chemical formula for the table salt we use every day is NaCl, which stands for sodium chloride!

What is the main chemical found in chalk and limestone?

It is calcium carbonate! Its chemical formula is CaCO3.
Did you know chalk and limestone are made of calcium carbonate? Its cool chemical formula is CaCO3!
Sodium hydroxide is also known as lye or caustic soda. Its chemical formula is simply written as NaOH!

briefs.competency: explain how plate tectonics can be used to explain the formation of the largest mountain ranges on Earth including the Himalayas and the Andes mountains
existing_facts_en: Mountain ranges form at continental-continental convergent boundaries when two continents collide and their edges crumple, fold, and push upward over millions of years.

How did the tallest mountains on Earth form?

The Himalayas formed when India and Eurasia, two large landmasses, collided about 40 to 50 million years ago and their crust crumpled upward.
When two plates push together, Earth's crust crumples and rises up — forming giant mountains like the Himalayas!
When two giant pieces of Earth's crust called tectonic plates collide, the land gets pushed up to form mountains!

How did the world's tallest mountains form?

The tallest peaks, like Mount Everest, were created when two giant continents crashed into each other!
When two tectonic plates crash into each other, they push the ground up to build huge mountains!

How does convection help build mountains?

Mantle convection pushes the plates! Some plates collide and crumple the crust upward — that's how great mountain ranges like the Himalayas form.
Mountain ranges form when tectonic plates slowly push together! Over a long time, land folds upward. It is very slow, just like your fingernails grow!
The Himalayas in Asia have the world's tallest peaks, including Mount Everest! They formed when India's plate crashed into Asia's plate — and they're still slowly rising today!
Mountains form when huge pieces of the Earth's crust slowly push against each other over millions of years, pushing the ground up. Some also come from volcanoes!
Many mountains form when huge pieces of Earth's crust slowly push against each other, lifting the land upward!

Most Philippine mountain ranges, like Sierra Madre and Cordillera, formed by tectonic uplift: when plates converge, land is pushed upward. These mountains still rise a few millimetres each year as plates collide!

What happens when plates crash into each other?

At a convergent boundary, plates push and collide! This creates tall mountains, deep trenches, and lots of earthquakes and volcanoes.
When two continental plates crash together, neither sinks! Both are too light, so the crust crumples upward — building giant mountains like the Himalayas!
Mount Everest grows about four millimeters taller every year because tectonic plates are still pushing it upward!

briefs.competency: identify and explain that to change the momentum of an object, it is necessary to apply a force on the object over a period of time
existing_facts_en: Impulse is force multiplied by the time it acts! This is exactly what causes a change in an object's momentum.
Stretch out the time of an impact, and the force you feel gets smaller! Same momentum change, but much safer!
A crumple zone is the part of a car designed to crush and fold in a crash! This makes the impact take longer, lowering the force on passengers.
In a crash, an airbag inflates fast to give your head and chest more time to stop, making the hitting force much smaller!

Why is it harder to stop heavy or fast objects?

Because they have greater momentum! This means you need a larger force or a longer time to bring them fully to a stop.
Force is how quickly an object's momentum changes, so the faster you change its momentum, the larger the force required!
The change in an object's momentum depends on how strong the force is and how long that force acts!
An airbag makes your body stop more slowly during a crash, so the push on you feels much softer and safer!
When a car crashes and stops suddenly, your body keeps its forward momentum! The seatbelt holds you tight, slowly reducing your momentum so you don't hit hard.

How do the thick boxing gloves protect your hands from getting hurt during a punch?

The thick padding in boxing gloves stretches out the time of a punch's impact! This lowers the force at each instant and reduces injury.

Why do baseball players swing and 'follow through' after hitting the ball?

It's not just force strength — it's HOW LONG it acts! A longer contact means a bigger change in motion. Follow-through keeps your bat on the ball longer so it flies farther!

What is impulse, and how does it change momentum?

Impulse equals force multiplied by time! It changes an object's momentum. The longer you apply force, the bigger the change in momentum!
Crumple zones in cars extend collision time! Since impulse equals force times time, a longer collision means less force hits the passengers — keeping them safer!
In an egg drop, soft padding makes the egg stop more slowly. This lessens the impact force so your egg stays safe and does not break!

Why should you bend your knees when landing from a jump?

It increases impact time, reducing the physical force on your leg bones and preventing fractures!

briefs.competency: participate in guided activities to explore and record how and when the Sun, the Moon, planets, and stars can be seen moving across the sky
existing_facts_en:
Where does the sun set every day?

The sun always sets in the West!
The Moon rises about an hour later each day because it keeps moving along its orbit around Earth!

Do stars really move across the night sky?

They seem to move from east to west, but it’s actually the Earth turning, not the stars themselves!

Do star patterns change every night?

Nope! Star patterns stay the same each night. They just seem to drift slowly from east to west as the Earth turns!
A constellation is a star pattern that draws a picture in the sky! These same star pictures slowly move across the night sky every evening.
Just like the Sun, the Moon rises in the east and sets in the west because of Earth's rotation!

Is Orion really moving across the sky?

It looks like Orion rises in the east and sets in the west! But it's not really moving—it's our Earth turning that makes Orion appear to travel across the sky.
The North Star (Polaris) stays almost still while other stars circle the night sky! It always points north, so long ago, sailors and travelers used it to find direction without a map!

Why do stars seem to move across the night sky?

They aren't really moving; Earth is spinning! As our planet turns, the sky shifts, making stars rise in the east and set in the west, just like the Sun does.

Do constellations disappear when we can't see them?

Nope! They're still up there, just hiding on the Sun's side. They rise with the Sun in daytime, so its bright light washes them out of our night view.
A constellation rises about 4 minutes earlier each night. Tiny, right? But over a month, it adds up to 2 hours! That's why evening stars slowly swap out through the year.

How can you spot the changing constellations?

Look at the sky at the exact same time every few nights! You'll see constellations slowly shift westward, proving that Earth orbits the Sun!

Why does the Sun always rise in the east and set in the west?

Earth spins toward the east! This makes the Sun look like it's moving the opposite way across the sky, rising in the east and setting in the west.

Why do stars look like they're moving?

The stars aren't actually moving! Earth is rotating, which keeps changing our view of space and makes the stars seem to circle across the sky.

Does the Sun really move across the sky?

The Sun seems to rise in the east and set in the west — but it's really Earth spinning, not the Sun moving!

briefs.competency: carry out simple investigations to demonstrate that contact forces cause objects to move in the same direction as the direction that the force is applied
existing_facts_en:
Where exactly does an object go when a force acts on it? Let's explore the science!

Every force has a direction! An object moves toward where it is pushed or pulled.
If you tilt your hand out of a moving car window, the air pushes it upward! This is the exact same way lift works on a wing.

Who wins in a game of tug-of-war?

The side that pulls with greater force wins and drags the other side!

Which way will an object move when pushed or pulled?

Every force has a direction! An object moves in the direction of the push or pull.

Do you push water down to make the boat go forward?

Nope! To go forward, you must push water BACKWARD, not down. Pushing down only lifts the boat a little — it won't move ahead!
In shallow water, use a long pole instead of a paddle! Push it against the mud or rocks below. Pushing the ground gives a stronger forward push than pushing water.
For the strongest push, keep the paddle almost vertical (straight up-and-down) as you pull! If it's too flat, the force just lifts water instead of driving the boat forward.
A kalesa is a carriage pulled by a horse—the horse uses muscle power to apply force and make the wheels roll!

What happens in marbles when one rolling marble hits a still one?

In marbles, the moving marble transfers its motion to the other, so the struck marble rolls away!
When fishermen haul their net back to the boat, they use a pulling force to move the heavy net full of fish!
Friction between your rubber shoes and the ground pushes you forward when you walk, proving friction can cause motion, not just stop it!
Did you know friction can speed things up? A moving conveyor belt uses friction to quickly speed up a stationary box placed right on top of it!

How does a carabao pull a heavy sled through a muddy field?

The carabao uses its super-strong force to pull the heavy sled through the mud!

How do you keep the ball flying in the game of sipa?

Players use a strong upward kicking force to accelerate the woven rattan ball and keep it airborne!
When one jolen marble hits another, it passes on a force to make it roll away! It gradually slows down because of friction with the ground.

briefs.competency: distinguish among comets, meteoroids, asteroids, and dwarf planets, and describe how they help us to understand the nature and formation of the Earth and the Solar System
existing_facts_en: Asteroids are composed mainly of rock and metals such as silicate, iron, and nickel.
Comet orbits are highly elliptical, while asteroid orbits are more rounded and less elliptical.

What are asteroids, and why do scientists study them?

Asteroids are leftover building blocks from when our solar system first formed billions of years ago! They never became part of a planet, so scientists study them to learn how planets formed.
An asteroid is mostly rock and metal with no tail, while a comet has lots of ice and gas that turns into a shining tail when it nears the Sun. So it is the comet that has the tail, not the asteroid!

What makes Ceres a 'dwarf planet' instead of just an asteroid?

It's the biggest object in the asteroid belt and is so large it's almost perfectly round! That's why scientists call it a dwarf planet, not just an asteroid.
A comet is full of ice, so it grows a cool tail! An asteroid is mostly rock or metal and has no tail at all.

Where do asteroids and meteoroids come from?

Many are leftover pieces from when the Solar System formed billions of years ago!

Did comets bring water to Earth?

A leading theory says comets and asteroids brought water during the Late Heavy Bombardment! But the Rosetta mission found comet 67P's water has a different chemical signature, complicating this idea.
An asteroid is made of rock and metal, while a comet is made of ice, dust, and rock!
A meteoroid is a cool rock floating in space that has not yet entered Earth's atmosphere!
Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and is also considered a dwarf planet!

Are meteorites older than the Earth?

Most meteorites that land on Earth are actually older than our planet! They formed at the solar system's very beginning.
A dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is round from its own gravity. But it hasn't cleared its orbit of other objects, so it's not a full planet!
Comets are made of ice and dust—they grow a tail near the Sun! Asteroids are rockier and metallic, with no tail at all.
Scientists study asteroids and comets because they barely changed in billions of years, acting like "fossils" that preserve our solar system's formation history!

briefs.competency: describe the trophic levels of an organism as levels of energy in a food pyramid
existing_facts_en: Biomass is the total mass of organic molecules minus water in an organism, and it decreases as you go up each trophic level.
Only about 10% of the energy at one feeding level passes to the next; the rest is used up for breathing and moving, or lost as heat.
At each step of a food chain, a lot of energy is lost as heat — so less and less gets passed on to the next animal.

Why is most food chain energy lost?

At each step in a food chain, only about 10% of the energy passes to the next level — the other 90% is lost as heat!

Why is there no predator above the top predator?

Almost nothing eats the topmost predator — there's simply too little energy left over to support yet another level in the food chain.
In the ocean, tiny plankton form the huge base of the food pyramid, while sharks at the very top are far fewer in number.

Why is an energy pyramid pyramid-shaped?

An energy pyramid is wide at the bottom, where producers are, and narrow at the top, because energy is lost at each level of the food chain.

Why are there so few top predators?

Less and less energy reaches each higher level of a food chain, so only a few big predators can be supported at the very top.

Why is the energy pyramid wide at the bottom?

Because less and less energy is available at each higher level — that's why it's wide at the bottom and narrow at the top!

Why is the top of an energy pyramid always smallest?

It measures how much energy is stored at each level — and that's exactly why the top level is always the tiniest!
There are so many plants at the base of the food pyramid because they're the starting source of energy for every other living thing.
At each level of a food chain, energy shrinks because animals use it to move and breathe, and much escapes as heat — that's why only a few big predators reach the top.

Why are there fewer predators than plants?

It's not just luck — predators are few and plants are many because energy is lost at every level of the food chain.

Why are there fewer predators than plants?

There are usually fewer predators at the top of the food chain than plants at the bottom, because energy gets smaller and smaller as it moves up.
Energy doesn't get recycled back through the food pyramid -- fresh energy from the sun must keep arriving.

Why are there so few big predators?

Only a little energy is left at the top of the food pyramid, so there's barely enough to support large predators — that's why there are so few!

briefs.competency: differentiate the subatomic particles protons, neutrons, and electrons in terms of their symbol, mass, charge, and location within an atom
existing_facts_en:
What are the three smaller parts that make up an atom?

Protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge) sit in the center, while electrons (negative) move around the outside!
Protons and neutrons are much heavier than electrons, which are extremely light and tiny!
An atom has three main particles! Positive protons and neutral neutrons hang out in the nucleus, while negative electrons zoom around it.
Atoms are tiny, but they have even smaller parts! Inside are protons and neutrons in the center nucleus, with electrons moving around the outside.
An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus with protons and neutrons, surrounded by an electron cloud. Amazingly, more than 99.9% of its volume is just empty space!

What three subatomic particles make up an atom?

Protons with a positive charge in the nucleus, neutrons with no charge in the nucleus, and electrons with a negative charge orbiting the nucleus!

Does a neutron have a charge?

Nope! A neutron has no charge at all. It is completely neutral, which means its charge is zero!
The electron is the lightest of the three particles! It is about 1,800 times lighter than a proton. Wow, that's super light!

Who discovered the neutral neutron?

James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932! This tiny particle has no electrical charge and lives inside the atom's nucleus.
Here is the neutron! It has absolutely no charge at all, making it perfectly neutral.
The proton and neutron are like twins when it comes to weight—they have nearly the same mass!

Which subatomic particle is the absolute lightest of the three?

The electron! It is the lightest of the three subatomic particles.
A proton is a particle with a positive (+) charge found in the atom's center, or nucleus, and it has nearly the same mass as a neutron!

What does a neutron do inside the nucleus?

A neutron has no charge (neutral) and weighs about the same as a proton, so it adds to the atom's mass!
An electron is a super light particle with a negative (−) charge zooming around the nucleus! It's almost 2,000 times lighter than a proton or neutron.
In static electricity, the light electrons move, not the heavier protons that stay in the atom!

briefs.competency: explain that the arrangement of elements in the periodic table as 7 periods and 18 groups is based on their atomic structure and chemical properties, such as reactivity
existing_facts_en: Chlorine has the electron configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5, with seven valence electrons, placing it in group 17 of the periodic table.

Why are noble gases so special?

Noble gases like helium and neon are in the last column of the periodic table. They rarely react, so helium safely fills balloons and neon glows in signs!

Where are metals and nonmetals on the periodic table?

Most metals are on the left side and middle, while nonmetals are found in the upper right part.
Elements in the periodic table are arranged by atomic number! This is simply the number of protons in their atoms.
The vertical columns in the periodic table are called groups! Elements in the same group share similar properties.
The noble gases live in Group 18 of the periodic table, and they almost never react with other elements!

Where do halogens live on the periodic table?

The halogens are in Group 17! They are highly reactive nonmetals.
Noble gases are completely unreactive because their outer electron shell is already totally full!

How are elements arranged in the periodic table?

They are arranged by increasing atomic number! This means they are sorted by how many protons are in their nucleus.

What do we call the horizontal rows in the periodic table?

They are called periods! The main periodic table has exactly seven periods from left to right.

What are the vertical columns of the periodic table called?

They are called groups! Elements found in the same group share very similar chemical properties.
Noble gases like helium, neon, and argon are in Group 18. They almost never react because their outer electron shell is already full!
Halogens like fluorine and chlorine are in Group 17. They are reactive nonmetals that have exactly seven valence electrons!

Why are alkali metals like sodium and potassium so reactive in Group 1?

They are very reactive because they have just one valence electron!

What happens to alkali metals as you go down their group?

They become more reactive! That's why potassium reacts more violently with water than sodium does.

Why is hydrogen treated as a special element?

Although it sits at the top of Group 1, it is a nonmetal and unlike the alkali metals!

briefs.competency: explain the formation of ions as either the loss or gain of electrons to produce ionic bonds, using examples, such as the formation of sodium chloride
existing_facts_en:
What happens when an atom loses or gains an electron?

It becomes charged and is called an ion!

What happens to electrons when an ionic bond forms?

Metal atoms tend to lose electrons, while nonmetal atoms tend to gain them!
When an atom loses an electron, it becomes a positive ion called a cation! If it gains an electron, it becomes a negative ion called an anion.

How does a neutral atom become an ion?

It becomes an ion when its number of electrons changes, so the electrons and protons no longer match!
When salt forms, sodium gives one electron to chlorine! Sodium becomes a positive ion, and chlorine becomes a negative ion.

How do atoms stick together in table salt?

In an ionic bond, one atom gives electrons to another, giving them opposite charges that attract—like sodium and chlorine in sodium chloride!

How does an ionic bond form?

When a metal atom GIVES its electron to a nonmetal atom! After this, both become charged and attract each other.
In IONIC bonds, electrons are GIVEN away by metals to nonmetals. But in COVALENT bonds, nonmetals SHARE electrons, just like in water! They join in totally different ways.

What are the two types of ions in an ionic compound?

The CATION is positive because a metal lost an electron. The ANION is negative because a nonmetal gained one. They always come together as a pair!
Atoms give away electrons to be stable! This means having a FULL outer shell of 8 electrons. Giving or taking electrons helps them reach this stable state.

Is a piece of pure metal an ionic compound?

Nope! A pure metal alone is just an ELEMENT, not a compound. A nonmetal must join and exchange electrons first before an ionic compound can form!
An ionic bond forms when atoms transfer electrons, like in NaCl (table salt). A covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons, like in H2O (water)!
When an atom loses electrons, it becomes a positively charged ion called a cation! A great example is the sodium ion, Na⁺.
When an atom gains extra electrons, it becomes a negatively charged ion called an anion! A common example is the chloride ion, Cl⁻.

What happens when an atom loses or gains electrons?

It becomes charged and is called an ion! It is positive if it loses electrons, and negative if it gains them.
In chemistry, a salt isn't just table salt — it's any ionic compound made when the positive ion from a base joins the negative ion from an acid!

briefs.competency: explain how the subduction of an oceanic plate impacts on the plate above it
existing_facts_en: Along the Ring of Fire, one tectonic plate sinks under another in subduction, melting rock into magma to feed volcanoes!

How does subduction create volcanoes?

When a plate sinks beneath another, it melts into magma that rises up and builds volcanoes on the surface!
When one plate sinks beneath another, it melts in Earth's heat and forms new magma that can feed a volcano!

What happens when one tectonic plate slides under another?
